cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 10-year-old girl has involuntary, jerky, purposeless movements, emotional lability and "milkmaid's grip" 3 months after a sore throat. ASO titre is normal. What is the diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Chorea may appear months after streptococcal infection when ASO has normalised; it alone is sufficient for ARF diagnosis; needs secondary prophylaxis and echo.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 9-year-old has acute rheumatic fever with polyarthritis and mild carditis. What is the treatment for the arthritis?
o: Aspirin (or naproxen) and eradication of streptococci with penicillin
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: NSAIDs produce dramatic response in ARF arthritis; steroids are reserved for severe carditis with heart failure.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Which clinical sign is most useful for detecting heart failure in an infant?
o: Hepatomegaly with tachypnoea, sweating and poor feeding
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Infants rarely have peripheral oedema or visible JVP; hepatomegaly and feeding difficulty are key signs.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 6-week-old baby has poor feeding, pallor and heart rate 260/min with narrow QRS and no visible P waves. Baby is haemodynamically stable. What is the first manoeuvre?
o: Ice-water bag applied to the face (diving reflex)
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: In infants, facial ice application; then IV adenosine (100 microgram/kg, increasing). Eyeball pressure is dangerous; verapamil is contraindicated in infants.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A boy has short stature, webbed neck, low-set ears, pectus excavatum and normal karyotype. Which cardiac lesion is most common?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Noonan syndrome (PTPN11, autosomal dominant) – pulmonary stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A girl with short stature, webbed neck and lymphoedema of the feet at birth has a 45,XO karyotype. Which cardiac lesions are typical?
o: Bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of aorta
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Turner syndrome: coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve with aortic dilatation; monitor with echo/MRI.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A child with "elfin" facies, overfriendly personality, hypercalcaemia and learning difficulty has a murmur. Which cardiac lesion is characteristic?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Williams syndrome is due to 7q11.23 deletion (elastin gene); also peripheral pulmonary stenosis.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Which cardiac abnormalities are more common in infants of diabetic mothers?
o: Transposition of great arteries, VSD and asymmetric septal hypertrophy
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Poor glycaemic control causes septal hypertrophy (usually transient) and structural defects including TGA and VSD.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A fetus is found to have bradycardia of 55/min at 22 weeks. The mother has dry eyes and mouth. Which maternal antibody is responsible?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Transplacental anti-Ro/La damage the fetal conduction system; neonatal lupus may also cause rash and cytopenias.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Maternal use of which drug in the first trimester is associated with Ebstein anomaly?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Ebstein anomaly: apical displacement of the tricuspid valve with "atrialisation" of RV; associated with WPW. Absolute risk with lithium is lower than earlier thought.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A neonate with obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return has severe cyanosis and respiratory distress. Chest X-ray shows a small heart with pulmonary venous congestion. What is the treatment?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Obstructed TAPVR is a surgical emergency; PGE1 does not help and may worsen pulmonary oedema. Unobstructed supracardiac type gives "snowman" appearance.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A cyanotic infant has ECG showing left axis deviation and left ventricular hypertrophy. Which lesion is most likely?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Cyanosis with left axis deviation and LVH strongly suggests tricuspid atresia (hypoplastic RV); TOF has right axis deviation and RVH.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Newborn pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart disease is considered positive when:
o: SpO₂ 97% in right hand and 96% in foot
SpO₂ <90% in any limb, or <95% in both right hand and foot on repeated measures, or >3% difference between them
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Pre-ductal (right hand) and post-ductal (foot) saturations after 24 hours detect duct-dependent lesions before collapse.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 5-year-old with uncorrected cyanotic heart disease presents with fever, headache, vomiting and new focal seizures. What complication must be suspected?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Right-to-left shunts bypass pulmonary filtration; brain abscess is common after 2 years. Under 2, cerebral venous thrombosis/stroke from polycythaemia is more likely.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Why is iron deficiency harmful in a child with cyanotic heart disease?
o: Microcytic red cells are less deformable, increasing hyperviscosity and stroke risk
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Relative iron deficiency despite high Hb increases risk of cerebrovascular events; iron supplementation is given.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 10-year-old with repaired TOF with prosthetic conduit has fever for 2 weeks, splenomegaly and microscopic haematuria. What is the most important investigation?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Children with CHD and prosthetic material are at high risk for IE; modified Duke criteria apply.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 4-year-old has sudden tachycardia out of proportion to fever, gallop rhythm, hepatomegaly and cardiomegaly after a viral illness. ECG shows low voltage and ST changes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Coxsackie B and adenovirus are common causes; supportive HF management; IVIG use is controversial.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: An unvaccinated 6-year-old with a greyish adherent pharyngeal membrane and "bull neck" develops bradycardia and heart block in the second week. What is the cause?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Diphtheria exotoxin causes myocarditis (week 2) and neuropathy (palatal palsy); give antitoxin early plus penicillin/erythromycin.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: What is the recommended compression-to-ventilation ratio for single healthcare-provider CPR in a child?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: European Resuscitation Council: 5 rescue breaths, then 15:2 for healthcare professionals (30:2 acceptable for lay rescuers).

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Which chest compression technique is recommended for two rescuers performing CPR on an infant?
o: Two-thumb encircling technique on the lower third of the sternum
Two hands on the lower sternum
One finger over the left chest
Heel of one hand on upper sternum
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Compression depth is at least one-third of chest AP diameter (~4 cm infant, ~5 cm child).

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old child (12 kg) is in septic shock without signs of fluid overload. What is the initial fluid bolus?
o: 10–20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid (120–240 mL), reassessing after each bolus
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Current guidance favours 10–20 mL/kg boluses with reassessment for hepatomegaly/crackles; avoid boluses in severe malnutrition and in settings without intensive care (FEAST).

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: What is the dose of adrenaline in paediatric cardiac arrest?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Maximum single dose 1 mg; repeat every 3–5 minutes.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 14-year-old boy has sharp, localised left chest pain reproduced by pressing on the costochondral junctions. ECG and examination are otherwise normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Most chest pain in children is non-cardiac; red flags are exertional pain/syncope, abnormal ECG or family history of sudden death.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 10-year-old boy has BP 150/95 mmHg in the right arm and weak femoral pulses. What is the next best investigation?
o: Echocardiography (and four-limb BP) to evaluate for coarctation of the aorta
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: In children, hypertension is more often secondary (renal parenchymal, renovascular, coarctation); upper–lower limb BP difference suggests coarctation.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old has isolated severe valvular pulmonary stenosis with a gradient of 70 mmHg. What is the treatment of choice?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Balloon valvuloplasty is highly effective for typical (non-dysplastic) valvular PS with gradient >40–50 mmHg.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A neonate with 22q11.2 deletion has heart failure, mild cyanosis, bounding pulses and a single S2. Echo shows one great artery arising from both ventricles over a VSD. What is the diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Truncus arteriosus is strongly associated with DiGeorge syndrome; early surgical repair before pulmonary vascular disease.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A child with heart failure on digoxin develops vomiting, bradycardia and ectopics. Which factor most increases the risk of toxicity?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity; monitor K⁺ and levels.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 15-year-old collapses and dies during a football match. Autopsy shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with myocyte disarray. What is the recommended action for his family?
o: Clinical screening (ECG, echocardiography) and genetic testing of first-degree relatives
Start beta-blockers in all family members
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: HCM is autosomal dominant (sarcomeric genes); cascade screening identifies at-risk relatives.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 7-year-old with purulent pericarditis from Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia has signs of tamponade. What is the essential treatment?
o: Urgent pericardial drainage plus IV antistaphylococcal antibiotics
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Purulent pericarditis is life-threatening and needs drainage (often surgical) and IV antibiotics.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Why should a large VSD with heart failure be surgically closed within the first year of life?
o: To prevent irreversible pulmonary vascular obstructive disease (Eisenmenger syndrome)
Because the VSD will always enlarge
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Irreversible pulmonary hypertension can develop by 1–2 years; surgery is usually done at 3–6 months if HF fails medical therapy.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: What does a modified Blalock–Taussig shunt connect?
o: Superior vena cava to pulmonary artery
Inferior vena cava to pulmonary artery
Subclavian (or innominate) artery to the pulmonary artery
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: A palliative systemic-to-pulmonary shunt to increase pulmonary blood flow in cyanotic lesions with reduced pulmonary flow; Glenn connects SVC to PA.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: In a Fontan circulation, how does systemic venous blood reach the lungs?
o: Passively via direct connection of vena cavae to pulmonary arteries, without a ventricular pump
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Fontan physiology depends on low pulmonary vascular resistance; complications include protein-losing enteropathy, liver disease and arrhythmias.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Which ECG finding is normal in a healthy newborn but abnormal in an adult?
o: Right axis deviation with dominant R wave in V1
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Right ventricular dominance at birth reflects fetal circulation; it shifts toward adult pattern over the first year.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 4-year-old has a continuous murmur below the right clavicle heard in sitting that disappears on lying flat or turning the head. What is it?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Venous hum is due to turbulent jugular venous flow; it disappears when supine or with jugular compression.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-month-old with large VSD and heart failure is failing to thrive. Which is the initial medical therapy?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Caloric supplementation (fortified or NG feeds) and diuretics; ACE inhibitors are sometimes added; surgical repair if failure persists.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-month-old has hypotonia, macroglossia, massive cardiomegaly with short PR and huge QRS complexes. Which enzyme is deficient?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Infantile Pompe (glycogen storage disease type II) causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; enzyme replacement (alglucosidase alfa) improves survival.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-month-old has irritability and sweating during feeds, dilated cardiomyopathy and ECG shows deep Q waves in I and aVL. What is the likely diagnosis?
o: Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA)
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: ALCAPA causes myocardial ischaemia as pulmonary pressure falls after birth; "infant angina" during feeding; surgical reimplantation.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A cyanotic neonate has decreased pulmonary markings on X-ray. Which lesion is duct-dependent for pulmonary blood flow?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Duct-dependent pulmonary circulation: pulmonary atresia, critical PS, severe TOF, tricuspid atresia; duct-dependent systemic: HLHS, critical coarctation, interrupted arch, critical AS.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 4-month-old has coryza for 2 days followed by cough, tachypnoea, subcostal recession, widespread fine crackles and wheeze during winter. SpO₂ is 94% and feeding is adequate. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Supportive care: nasal suction, small frequent feeds and monitoring; no bronchodilators or steroids
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: RSV bronchiolitis: evidence does not support routine bronchodilators, steroids or antibiotics; oxygen if SpO₂ <90–92%; nasogastric feeds if intake <50%.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Which agent is used to prevent severe RSV disease in high-risk infants?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Long-acting nirsevimab (single dose) and maternal RSVpreF vaccine are newer strategies; palivizumab requires monthly doses.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old has barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor at rest since last night after coryza. He is not drooling and is not toxic. What is the first-line treatment?
o: Single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (nebulised adrenaline if severe)
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Croup (parainfluenza) causes subglottic narrowing (steeple sign); steroids reduce severity; nebulised adrenaline for severe stridor with observation for rebound.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: An unvaccinated 4-year-old has high fever, drooling, muffled voice, soft stridor and sits leaning forward. What should be AVOIDED?
o: Giving IV ceftriaxone after securing the airway
Calling an anaesthetist and ENT surgeon
Keeping the child with the parent
Examining the throat or lying the child down
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Acute epiglottitis (Hib) risks sudden complete airway obstruction; secure airway by experienced anaesthetist; thumb sign on lateral neck X-ray.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old with apparent croup becomes toxic with high fever, copious purulent secretions and no response to nebulised adrenaline. What is the diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Bacterial tracheitis requires airway support (often intubation) and IV antibiotics covering S. aureus.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: An 18-month-old had a sudden choking episode while eating peanuts, followed by cough and unilateral wheeze. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation of the right lung on expiratory film. What is the management?
o: Rigid bronchoscopy to remove the foreign body
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Ball-valve obstruction causes air trapping; right main bronchus is commonest site; rigid bronchoscopy under GA.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 6-month-old is conscious but unable to cry or cough after choking on a small object. What is the recommended first action?
o: Up to 5 back blows with the infant head-down along your forearm, followed by up to 5 chest thrusts
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Abdominal thrusts are avoided in infants due to risk of visceral injury; start CPR if unresponsive.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: According to WHO IMCI, fast breathing in a child aged 2–12 months is defined as:
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: <2 months ≥60; 2–12 months ≥50; 12 months–5 years ≥40 breaths/min.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 14-month-old has cough, RR 48/min and lower chest wall indrawing. There are no general danger signs and SpO₂ is 95%. According to revised WHO/IMCI guidelines, what is the treatment?
o: Oral amoxicillin at home for 5 days with follow-up
IV ampicillin and gentamicin in all cases
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: WHO 2014 revision: chest indrawing without danger signs is "pneumonia" treated with oral amoxicillin; severe pneumonia (danger signs, SpO₂ <90%) needs referral and injectable antibiotics.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Which is a general danger sign in IMCI requiring urgent referral?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: General danger signs: unable to drink/breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargic or unconscious.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 10-month-old with measles develops rapidly progressive pneumonia with high fever. Chest X-ray shows pneumatoceles and a pyopneumothorax. Which organism is most likely?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: S. aureus pneumonia causes pneumatoceles, empyema and pneumothorax; cloxacillin (or vancomycin for MRSA) and drainage.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 6-week-old infant has staccato cough, tachypnoea, no fever and a history of conjunctivitis at 2 weeks. Blood shows eosinophilia. What is the treatment?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonitis presents at 1–3 months, afebrile; macrolides are used (watch for pyloric stenosis with erythromycin).

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-month-old unvaccinated infant has paroxysms of coughing ending in vomiting and apnoea, with lymphocytosis of 30 × 10⁹/L. What is the treatment of choice?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Macrolides reduce transmission; infants <6 months risk apnoea, pulmonary hypertension and death; maternal Tdap vaccination protects newborns.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old with measles in Pakistan develops pneumonia. Which supplement reduces mortality and complications?
o: Vitamin A on two consecutive days (100,000 IU for 6–11 months; 200,000 IU for ≥12 months)
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: WHO recommends vitamin A for all children with measles; pneumonia is the commonest cause of measles deaths.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: What is the most appropriate inhaler device for a 3-year-old child with asthma?
o: pMDI with spacer and face mask
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Under 4–5 years: pMDI + spacer with mask; older children use spacer with mouthpiece; DPIs need adequate inspiratory flow (usually >6 years).

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 7-year-old with acute asthma has SpO₂ 90%, cannot talk, uses accessory muscles and has RR 45/min. After oxygen and salbutamol with ipratropium, what should be given early?
o: Oral prednisolone (or IV hydrocortisone) and consider IV magnesium sulphate if poor response
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Life-threatening features in children include SpO₂ <92%, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, altered consciousness; IV MgSO₄ 40 mg/kg over 20 min.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old has wheeze only with viral colds, with no symptoms between episodes and no atopy. What is this phenotype called?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Episodic viral wheeze often resolves by school age; managed with SABA; montelukast or intermittent ICS may be tried.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 1-year-old has failure to thrive, bulky foul-smelling stools, recurrent chest infections and a history of meconium ileus. What is the diagnostic test?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: CF (CFTR mutation, autosomal recessive); newborn screening uses immunoreactive trypsinogen; CFTR modulators (elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor) have transformed care.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: Which organism colonising the lungs of an adolescent with cystic fibrosis is associated with accelerated decline and is a relative contraindication to lung transplantation in some centres?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: S. aureus and H. influenzae in early childhood, Pseudomonas later; B. cepacia complex causes rapid decline and cross-infection.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 4-year-old whose grandfather has smear-positive TB has weight loss, fever for 3 weeks and hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray. She cannot expectorate sputum. Which sample is most useful for bacteriological confirmation?
o: Gastric aspirate or induced sputum (or stool) for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Children rarely produce sputum; WHO endorses Xpert Ultra on gastric aspirate, induced sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirate or stool.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old asymptomatic child lives with his mother who has newly diagnosed smear-positive pulmonary TB. Chest X-ray is normal. What is recommended?
o: TB preventive treatment (e.g., 3HR or 6H) after excluding active disease
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: WHO recommends TPT for all household contacts under 5 years without active TB, regardless of test results.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A child has chronic wet cough, recurrent otitis media, chronic sinusitis and dextrocardia. What is the diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: PCD: situs inversus in ~50%; nasal nitric oxide is low; bronchiectasis and infertility develop.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 29-week preterm neonate develops grunting, recession and cyanosis within hours of birth. Chest X-ray shows diffuse ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms. What is the key treatment?
o: CPAP with endotracheal/less invasive surfactant administration
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: RDS is surfactant deficiency; antenatal corticosteroids reduce incidence; LISA/INSURE techniques deliver surfactant.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A woman in preterm labour at 30 weeks is admitted. What is given to reduce neonatal RDS?
o: IV hydrocortisone to the baby after birth
IM betamethasone 12 mg two doses 24 hours apart (or dexamethasone 6 mg 4 doses 12 hours apart)
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Antenatal corticosteroids between 24–34 weeks reduce RDS, IVH, NEC and mortality; MgSO₄ <32 weeks is for fetal neuroprotection.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A term baby born by elective caesarean section has tachypnoea (RR 80/min) with minimal distress. Chest X-ray shows fluid in horizontal fissure and prominent perihilar streaking. What is the diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Delayed clearance of lung fluid; resolves within 24–72 hours with supportive care.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A post-term baby born through thick meconium-stained liquor develops severe respiratory distress. Chest X-ray shows patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation. Which complication is most feared?
o: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: MAS causes airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, surfactant inactivation and PPHN; routine tracheal suctioning of non-vigorous babies is no longer recommended.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A term neonate with severe hypoxaemia has pre-ductal SpO₂ 95% and post-ductal SpO₂ 80% with a structurally normal heart on echo. What is the specific therapy?
o: Inhaled nitric oxide with optimal ventilation
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Differential cyanosis reflects right-to-left ductal shunting; iNO is a selective pulmonary vasodilator; ECMO if refractory.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A newborn has severe respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen, and heart sounds best heard on the right side. What is the immediate management?
o: Endotracheal intubation and nasogastric decompression; avoid bag-mask ventilation
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Bag-mask ventilation distends herniated bowel; surgery is delayed until stabilised; pulmonary hypoplasia and PPHN determine outcome.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 30-week preterm baby has recurrent apnoeic episodes with bradycardia on day 5. Sepsis, hypoglycaemia and anaemia have been excluded. What is the drug of choice?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Caffeine stimulates respiratory centre and reduces BPD and neurodevelopmental impairment (CAP trial).

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A preterm infant born at 26 weeks still requires oxygen at 36 weeks postmenstrual age. What is the diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: BPD (chronic lung disease of prematurity) is defined by oxygen requirement at 36 weeks PMA; risk factors include barotrauma, oxygen toxicity and infection.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A term newborn is not breathing after drying and stimulation. Heart rate is 80/min. According to NRP/HBB, what is the next step?
o: Positive pressure ventilation with bag-mask at 40–60 breaths/min in room air
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: "Golden minute": start PPV within 60 seconds; compressions (3:1) only if HR <60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A newborn becomes cyanosed while feeding and pink when crying. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed through either nostril. What is the diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Neonates are obligate nasal breathers; oral airway (McGovern nipple) then surgical repair; association with CHARGE syndrome.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A newborn with polyhydramnios history has excessive frothy salivation, choking with feeds and a nasogastric tube coiling in the upper pouch on X-ray, with gas in the stomach. What is the diagnosis?
o: Oesophageal atresia with distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Commonest type (Gross C, ~85%); keep NPO, continuous upper pouch suction (Replogle tube), check for VACTERL anomalies.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 6-week-old has inspiratory stridor that worsens when lying supine, crying and feeding, but is thriving. What is the commonest cause?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Laryngomalacia is the commonest cause of chronic stridor in infants; usually resolves by 18–24 months; supraglottoplasty if severe.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: An unvaccinated 5-year-old from a rural area has fever, sore throat, a grey adherent membrane that bleeds when removed, and massive neck swelling. What is the most important treatment?
o: Diphtheria antitoxin as early as possible plus penicillin/erythromycin
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Antitoxin neutralises unbound toxin and should not await culture; airway protection and isolation; contacts need prophylaxis and vaccination.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 4-year-old with pneumococcal pneumonia has persistent fever for 7 days on IV antibiotics with dullness on the left. Ultrasound shows a loculated effusion with septations. What is the management?
o: Chest drain insertion with intrapleural fibrinolytics (urokinase) or VATS
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Loculated parapneumonic effusions need drainage with fibrinolytics or VATS; most children recover fully.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 5-year-old snores loudly with witnessed pauses, restless sleep, daytime hyperactivity and large tonsils. What is the first-line treatment?
o: CPAP as first line in all
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the main cause of paediatric OSA; untreated OSA causes behavioural problems, poor growth and cor pulmonale.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old has fever, neck stiffness with reluctance to extend the neck, drooling and muffled voice. Lateral neck X-ray shows widened prevertebral soft tissue. What is the diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Retropharyngeal lymph nodes are prominent in under-5s; CT confirms; IV antibiotics ± surgical drainage.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: A child has had three episodes of right middle lobe pneumonia in one year. What is the most important next step?
o: Investigate for localised cause (e.g., foreign body, bronchial compression by TB nodes) with CT/bronchoscopy
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe suggests localised obstruction; in different lobes suggests systemic causes (aspiration, immunodeficiency, CF, PCD).

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: In a child with severe pneumonia in a low-resource setting, WHO recommends giving oxygen when SpO₂ is below:
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: WHO: oxygen for SpO₂ <90% (some guidelines use <92–94% for emergency signs); pulse oximetry should be used in all children with severe pneumonia.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: An antenatal scan showed a cystic lung lesion; the neonate is asymptomatic. CT shows a multicystic lesion in the left lower lobe. What is the likely diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: CPAM (previously CCAM) may cause infection or malignancy; elective resection is often advised.

cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.s: An 8-year-old asthmatic has persistent sneezing, nasal itching, clear rhinorrhoea and "allergic salute". Which treatment is most effective for persistent moderate symptoms?
cardiorespiratory-iii/paediatrics.e: Intranasal steroids are the most effective treatment; controlling rhinitis improves asthma control.

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: After a road accident, a patient has paradoxical movement of a segment of the right chest wall with multiple rib fractures and hypoxia. What is the major cause of hypoxia?
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: Flail chest (≥2 fractures in ≥2 adjacent ribs) – hypoxia mostly from lung contusion; management: analgesia (epidural/nerve blocks), oxygen, ventilation if required.

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: A stab wound patient has a chest drain inserted draining 1600 mL of blood immediately. What is the next step?
o: CT chest and admit to ward
Insert a second chest drain and observe
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: Indications for thoracotomy: >1500 mL immediate drainage or >200 mL/h for 2–4 hours, or persistent transfusion requirement.

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: A patient with a stab wound to the left parasternal region has hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. FAST shows pericardial fluid. What is definitive management?
o: Emergency thoracotomy/sternotomy to repair the cardiac injury
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: Pericardiocentesis is only a temporising measure; penetrating cardiac injury needs surgical repair.

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: After a high-speed deceleration injury, chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum (>8 cm), loss of aortic knob and deviation of the NG tube to the right. What is the likely injury?
o: Traumatic aortic rupture at the isthmus (distal to left subclavian)
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: CT angiography confirms; management by endovascular stent grafting with strict BP control.

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: Where is the safe triangle for chest drain insertion?
o: Bordered by the lateral edge of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line at the level of the nipple (5th intercostal space), with apex below the axilla
Below the nipple in the midclavicular line
Seventh intercostal space posterior axillary line
Anterior to pectoralis major in the 3rd space
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: Insert just above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: A 64-year-old with a peripheral stage IA NSCLC is considered for lobectomy. Which preoperative test best predicts postoperative respiratory function?
o: Predicted postoperative FEV₁ and DLCO (with cardiopulmonary exercise testing if borderline)
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: ppoFEV₁ and ppoDLCO >60% indicate low risk; lower values require exercise testing (VO₂ max).

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: A 70-year-old with atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) has sudden onset of a pale, pulseless, cold, painful leg with paraesthesia. What is the most likely cause and immediate treatment?
o: Arterial embolism; IV heparin and urgent embolectomy
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold; paralysis and sensory loss indicate threatened limb requiring immediate revascularisation.

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: A 72-year-old smoker has an asymptomatic pulsatile abdominal mass. Ultrasound shows an infrarenal AAA of 5.8 cm. What is the recommended management?
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: Repair when AAA ≥5.5 cm in men (≥5.0 cm in women), growth >1 cm/year, or symptomatic.

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: A 75-year-old has sudden severe abdominal and back pain, collapse, BP 80/50 mmHg and a pulsatile mass. What is the correct approach to fluid resuscitation?
o: Aggressive fluids to normalise BP before surgery
CT scan first in all unstable patients
Permissive hypotension (target SBP ~70–90 mmHg) and immediate transfer to theatre
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: Permissive hypotension limits further bleeding; unstable patients with known AAA go directly to theatre.

cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.s: After an episode of forceful vomiting following a heavy meal, a 50-year-old man has severe chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema in the neck and a left pleural effusion. What is the diagnosis?
cardiorespiratory-iii/surgery.e: Mackler's triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema; confirm with water-soluble contrast swallow/CT; urgent surgery.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 60-year-old man's serum creatinine rises from a baseline of 1.0 mg/dL to 2.3 mg/dL over 48 hours, with urine output 0.4 mL/kg/h for 14 hours. What is his KDIGO AKI stage?
renal-iii/medicine.e: KDIGO stage 2: creatinine 2.0–2.9 × baseline or UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 h. Stage 3: ≥3× baseline, creatinine ≥4 mg/dL, UO <0.3 for ≥24 h, or RRT.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient with severe diarrhoea has oliguria. Urine sodium is 8 mmol/L, fractional excretion of sodium <1%, urine osmolality 650 mOsm/kg, and bland sediment. What is the most likely cause of AKI?
o: Prerenal azotaemia due to volume depletion
renal-iii/medicine.e: Prerenal: FENa <1%, concentrated urine, BUN:creatinine >20. ATN: FENa >2%, muddy brown granular casts, isosthenuric urine.

renal-iii/medicine.s: Which urine microscopy finding is characteristic of acute tubular necrosis?
o: Muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells
renal-iii/medicine.e: Red cell casts = glomerulonephritis; WBC casts = pyelonephritis/interstitial nephritis; fatty casts = nephrotic syndrome; broad waxy casts = CKD.

renal-iii/medicine.s: Ten days after starting omeprazole, a patient develops rising creatinine, fever, rash, eosinophilia and sterile pyuria with WBC casts. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: AIN culprits: PPIs, NSAIDs, beta-lactams, rifampicin, sulfonamides; stop the drug, consider steroids.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A labourer is rescued after being trapped under rubble for 12 hours. Urine is dark and dipstick positive for blood but microscopy shows no RBCs. CK is 80,000 U/L. What is the most important initial treatment?
o: Aggressive IV isotonic fluids targeting urine output ~200–300 mL/h
renal-iii/medicine.e: Myoglobinuria causes AKI; early fluids (ideally before extrication) prevent crush-related AKI; monitor K⁺ and compartment syndrome.

renal-iii/medicine.s: Which is an indication for urgent haemodialysis in AKI?
o: Refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ 7.2 mmol/L) despite medical therapy
Serum creatinine 3.0 mg/dL with good urine output
renal-iii/medicine.e: AEIOU: Acidosis (severe), Electrolytes (refractory K⁺), Intoxication (lithium, methanol, salicylates), Overload (refractory pulmonary oedema), Uraemia (pericarditis, encephalopathy).

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 58-year-old diabetic has eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m² and urine albumin–creatinine ratio 150 mg/g, persisting for 4 months. What is the KDIGO classification?
A type 2 diabetic has hypertension, eGFR 55 and albuminuria 400 mg/g despite ramipril at maximum dose. Which drug added next has proven renal and cardiovascular benefit?
o: Adding an ARB to the ACE inhibitor
renal-iii/medicine.e: KDIGO 2022: RAS blockade + SGLT2i; finerenone for residual albuminuria; dual RAS blockade increases hyperkalaemia and AKI.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient with CKD stage 4 has Hb 8.8 g/dL, ferritin 60 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 14%. What is the first step before erythropoiesis-stimulating agents?
o: Start erythropoietin immediately with target Hb 14 g/dL
Replete iron (IV iron preferred in advanced CKD)
renal-iii/medicine.e: ESA response requires adequate iron (ferritin >100–200, TSAT >20%); target Hb 10–11.5 g/dL (higher targets increase stroke risk).

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient on haemodialysis has high phosphate, low calcium and PTH 900 pg/mL. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Phosphate retention and reduced calcitriol drive PTH secretion; treat with phosphate binders, dietary restriction, active vitamin D and calcimimetics (cinacalcet).

renal-iii/medicine.s: A renal transplant recipient with long-standing dialysis history has persistently high PTH with hypercalcaemia despite good graft function. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Autonomous parathyroid hyperplasia after prolonged stimulation; treatment is parathyroidectomy or cinacalcet.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73m². What is the correct advice regarding metformin?
o: Switch to extended release at maximum dose
Stop metformin due to risk of lactic acidosis
renal-iii/medicine.e: Metformin: reduce dose if eGFR 30–45; stop if <30.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 22-year-old man has sudden-onset generalised oedema, 24-hour urine protein 8 g, albumin 1.8 g/dL, normal renal function and no haematuria. He recently started NSAIDs for back pain. Which renal biopsy finding is expected on electron microscopy?
o: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes with normal light microscopy
renal-iii/medicine.e: Minimal change disease is associated with NSAIDs and Hodgkin lymphoma; highly steroid-responsive.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 55-year-old man has nephrotic syndrome. Serum anti-PLA2R antibodies are strongly positive. What is the diagnosis and an important complication to watch for?
o: Primary membranous nephropathy; renal vein thrombosis
renal-iii/medicine.e: Anti-PLA2R is present in ~70% of primary MN; nephrotic hypercoagulability (antithrombin loss) causes renal vein thrombosis; secondary causes include malignancy, hepatitis B, SLE, drugs.

renal-iii/medicine.s: An obese man with HIV has nephrotic-range proteinuria and progressive renal decline. Biopsy shows collapsing glomerulopathy. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: HIVAN is associated with APOL1 risk alleles; ART and RAS blockade are the mainstay.

renal-iii/medicine.s: Why are patients with nephrotic syndrome prone to infections?
o: Urinary loss of immunoglobulins (IgG) and complement factors
renal-iii/medicine.e: Also hypercoagulability (loss of antithrombin III), hyperlipidaemia, AKI and hypothyroidism (loss of thyroxine-binding globulin).

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 24-year-old man has visible haematuria 1–2 days after an upper respiratory tract infection, with normal complement levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Synpharyngitic haematuria (within days) = IgA nephropathy; PSGN occurs 1–3 weeks after infection with low C3.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 30-year-old male smoker has haemoptysis, rapidly rising creatinine and red cell casts. Renal biopsy shows crescents with linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. What is the urgent treatment?
o: Plasma exchange with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide
renal-iii/medicine.e: Goodpasture (anti-GBM) disease targets type IV collagen α3 chain; urgent treatment preserves renal function.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 65-year-old woman has weight loss, arthralgia, rapidly progressive renal failure with red cell casts, and p-ANCA (anti-MPO) positivity. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic GN. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Pauci-immune GN = ANCA vasculitis; induction with steroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide (avacopan as steroid-sparing).

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient with chronic hepatitis C has nephrotic–nephritic syndrome, low C4, purpura and positive cryoglobulins. What is the renal lesion?
renal-iii/medicine.e: HCV-associated mixed cryoglobulinaemia causes MPGN; direct-acting antivirals treat the cause.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 35-year-old man with hypertension and flank pain has bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts on ultrasound. His father died of a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Which drug slows cyst growth in rapidly progressive disease?
renal-iii/medicine.e: ADPKD (PKD1/PKD2) associations: liver cysts, berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse; tolvaptan (V2 antagonist) slows eGFR decline.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 16-year-old boy has persistent microscopic haematuria, progressive renal impairment, bilateral sensorineural deafness and anterior lenticonus. What is the defect?
o: Type IV collagen (COL4A5) – X-linked Alport syndrome
renal-iii/medicine.e: Alport syndrome shows GBM splitting ("basket weave") on EM; ACE inhibitors slow progression.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient has serum Na⁺ 124 mmol/L, serum osmolality 260 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 450 mOsm/kg, urine Na⁺ 45 mmol/L, is clinically euvolaemic, with normal thyroid and adrenal function. What is the first-line treatment if mildly symptomatic?
renal-iii/medicine.e: SIADH: euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine; severe symptoms need hypertonic 3% saline.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient with chronic hyponatraemia (Na⁺ 108 mmol/L) is corrected to 128 mmol/L within 24 hours. Three days later he develops dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Limit correction to 8–10 mmol/L in 24 h (lower in high-risk: alcoholics, malnourished, hypokalaemia).

renal-iii/medicine.s: An elderly bedbound patient with dementia has Na⁺ 162 mmol/L and is clinically dehydrated. What is the correct approach?
o: Replace free water deficit gradually (e.g., 5% dextrose or 0.45% saline), lowering Na⁺ by no more than ~10 mmol/L per day
renal-iii/medicine.e: Rapid correction of chronic hypernatraemia risks cerebral oedema.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 25-year-old woman with Sjögren syndrome has recurrent kidney stones, hypokalaemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with urine pH persistently >5.5. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Type 1 RTA: inability to acidify urine; nephrocalcinosis; associated with Sjögren, SLE, amphotericin. Type 4: hyperkalaemia (hypoaldosteronism, diabetes).

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient with multiple myeloma has glycosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria and normal anion gap acidosis. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Proximal tubular dysfunction can be due to light chains, tenofovir, ifosfamide, Wilson disease, cystinosis.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient has K⁺ 2.6 mmol/L with muscle weakness and U waves on ECG. What must be corrected concurrently to allow potassium repletion?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Hypomagnesaemia causes renal K⁺ wasting; IV K⁺ should not exceed 10–20 mmol/h via peripheral line.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 28-year-old non-pregnant woman has dysuria and frequency for 2 days with no fever or loin pain. What is appropriate management?
o: Empirical short-course nitrofurantoin (5 days) or fosfomycin single dose
Urine culture and wait for results before any treatment
renal-iii/medicine.e: Uncomplicated lower UTI: nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin or pivmecillinam; fluoroquinolones are reserved.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 30-year-old woman has fever with rigors, right loin pain and vomiting. Urine shows pus cells and nitrites. She is unable to tolerate oral medication. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Admit, send urine and blood cultures, start IV ceftriaxone (or aminoglycoside), and ultrasound kidneys
renal-iii/medicine.e: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve renal tissue levels; imaging if septic, not improving in 48–72 h, or suspected obstruction.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A poorly controlled diabetic woman has severe sepsis and flank pain. CT shows gas in the renal parenchyma. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Life-threatening gas-forming infection (E. coli, Klebsiella) in diabetics; IV antibiotics, drainage, sometimes nephrectomy.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 35-year-old man has frequency, dysuria and haematuria for months. Repeated urine cultures show "sterile pyuria". IVU shows a calcified, small "putty kidney". What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Send 3 early-morning urine samples for AFB/culture/PCR; complications include ureteric stricture and thimble bladder.

renal-iii/medicine.s: Four months after renal transplantation, a patient on tacrolimus has rising creatinine. Tacrolimus levels are within range. What is the best investigation to diagnose acute rejection?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Biopsy differentiates T-cell–mediated rejection, antibody-mediated rejection (C4d, DSA), calcineurin inhibitor toxicity and BK virus nephropathy.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A transplant patient on tacrolimus is started on clarithromycin and develops tremor and AKI. What is the mechanism?
o: CYP3A4 inhibition increases tacrolimus levels, causing nephrotoxicity
renal-iii/medicine.e: CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides, azoles, diltiazem, grapefruit) raise CNI levels; inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine) lower them.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 70-year-old on ramipril and furosemide develops AKI after taking diclofenac for knee pain. What is the mechanism?
o: Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation combined with ACEi-induced efferent dilatation ("triple whammy")
renal-iii/medicine.e: The combination of NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic markedly increases AKI risk in the elderly.

renal-iii/medicine.s: One week after coronary angiography, a 68-year-old develops AKI, livedo reticularis, blue toes, eosinophilia and low complement. What is the diagnosis?
o: Acute interstitial nephritis due to aspirin
renal-iii/medicine.e: Cholesterol emboli follow arterial instrumentation; delayed onset (days to weeks), eosinophilia and hypocomplementaemia distinguish it from contrast nephropathy (24–72 h).

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient with hypercalcaemia (calcium 13.8 mg/dL) is dehydrated and confused. What is the first-line treatment?
o: IV normal saline rehydration, then IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid)
renal-iii/medicine.e: Hypercalcaemia causes nephrogenic DI and volume depletion; saline first; calcitonin for rapid short-term effect; denosumab in renal impairment.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient on long-term lithium has polyuria, polydipsia and dilute urine that does not concentrate after desmopressin. What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Lithium downregulates aquaporin-2; thiazides and amiloride are used; no response to desmopressin distinguishes nephrogenic from cranial DI.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient on CAPD has cloudy effluent and abdominal pain. Effluent WBC is 300/µL with >50% neutrophils. What is the treatment?
o: Switch to haemodialysis and no antibiotics
Remove catheter immediately in all cases
Intraperitoneal antibiotics covering Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms after sending effluent culture
renal-iii/medicine.e: PD peritonitis is usually from skin organisms (S. epidermidis, S. aureus); intraperitoneal vancomycin/cefazolin + ceftazidime/aminoglycoside.

renal-iii/medicine.s: Which is the preferred long-term vascular access for haemodialysis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: AV fistulas have lowest infection and thrombosis rates; should be created months before dialysis is needed; protect the non-dominant arm from venepuncture.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient with ESRD not yet on dialysis develops a pericardial rub and chest pain. Urea is 280 mg/dL. What is the definitive treatment?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Uraemic pericarditis is an indication for urgent dialysis; heparin should be minimised due to haemorrhagic effusion risk.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A patient with atrial fibrillation has sudden flank pain, haematuria and markedly raised LDH with normal ALT. What is the likely diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Very high LDH with flank pain in AF suggests renal infarction; CT angiography confirms; anticoagulate.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A diabetic woman with chronic analgesic use passes tissue fragments in urine with colicky flank pain and haematuria. IVU shows a "ring shadow". What is the diagnosis?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Causes (POSTCARDS): pyelonephritis, obstruction, sickle cell, TB, cirrhosis, analgesics, renal vein thrombosis, diabetes, systemic vasculitis.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A CKD patient on ramipril has recurrent K⁺ of 5.8 mmol/L. Which newer agent allows continuation of RAAS blockade?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Novel K⁺ binders enable ongoing RAASi therapy; dietary potassium advice and treating acidosis (bicarbonate) also help.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A CKD stage 4 patient has serum bicarbonate 16 mmol/L. What is the recommended management?
o: Oral sodium bicarbonate supplementation to maintain bicarbonate ≥22 mmol/L
renal-iii/medicine.e: Correcting acidosis slows CKD progression and reduces bone loss and muscle wasting.

renal-iii/medicine.s: A 55-year-old smoker has painless visible haematuria with no infection. What is the most important investigation?
renal-iii/medicine.e: Painless visible haematuria in older adults requires exclusion of urothelial malignancy.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 35-year-old man has sudden severe left loin-to-groin colicky pain with microscopic haematuria. Which is the imaging investigation of choice?
renal-iii/urology.e: Low-dose non-contrast CT detects ~99% of stones; ultrasound is first-line in pregnancy and children.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 4 mm stone in the distal left ureter causes pain controlled with analgesia; renal function is normal and there is no infection. What is the management?
o: Analgesia (NSAIDs) and medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin, with follow-up imaging
renal-iii/urology.e: Stones <5 mm usually pass spontaneously; alpha-blockers help distal stones 5–10 mm; intervene if pain uncontrolled, infection, AKI or failure to pass.

renal-iii/urology.s: A patient with a 9 mm obstructing ureteric stone has fever 39°C, rigors and hypotension. What is the urgent management?
o: Resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent
renal-iii/urology.e: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency; definitive stone treatment is deferred until sepsis resolves.

renal-iii/urology.s: A woman with recurrent Proteus UTIs has a large staghorn calculus in the right renal pelvis. What is the stone composition and treatment of choice?
renal-iii/urology.e: Urease-producing organisms raise urine pH forming struvite; PCNL is first-line for large renal stones >2 cm.

renal-iii/urology.s: Which renal stone is radiolucent on plain X-ray and can be dissolved by urinary alkalinisation?
renal-iii/urology.e: Uric acid stones are radiolucent on X-ray but visible on CT; potassium citrate dissolves them.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 68-year-old man has nocturia, poor stream, hesitancy and terminal dribbling. DRE shows a smooth, enlarged, non-tender prostate estimated at 50 g. PSA is normal. IPSS is 18. What is appropriate initial medical treatment?
o: Alpha-1 blocker (tamsulosin) combined with 5-alpha reductase inhibitor (finasteride)
renal-iii/urology.e: Combination therapy is used for moderate–severe LUTS with prostate >30–40 g; 5-ARI takes 6 months and halves PSA.

renal-iii/urology.s: During TURP using glycine irrigation, a patient becomes confused, bradycardic and hypertensive with visual disturbance. What electrolyte abnormality is expected?
renal-iii/urology.e: Absorption of hypotonic irrigation fluid causes hyponatraemia and fluid overload; bipolar TURP with saline reduces risk.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 72-year-old man cannot pass urine for 12 hours, with a painful palpable bladder. What is the immediate management?
o: Urethral catheterisation, record residual volume, and start an alpha-blocker before trial without catheter
renal-iii/urology.e: Precipitants: BPH, constipation, anticholinergics, alcohol, infection; monitor for post-obstructive diuresis if residual >1 L.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 65-year-old man has PSA 28 ng/mL and a hard nodular prostate on DRE. What is the next investigation?
o: Multiparametric MRI prostate followed by targeted biopsy
renal-iii/urology.e: mpMRI before biopsy (PI-RADS) improves detection; staging with bone scan/PSMA PET for high-risk disease; Gleason/ISUP grade guides therapy.

renal-iii/urology.s: A patient with metastatic prostate cancer is started on a GnRH agonist (goserelin). Which drug should be given for the first weeks to prevent tumour flare?
renal-iii/urology.e: GnRH agonists cause an initial testosterone surge that can precipitate spinal cord compression or retention; GnRH antagonists (degarelix) avoid flare.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 58-year-old smoker has haematuria, flank pain, a palpable flank mass and a new left-sided varicocele that does not empty when supine. What is the likely diagnosis?
o: Left renal cell carcinoma with renal vein involvement
renal-iii/urology.e: Left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein; RCC may cause polycythaemia (EPO), hypercalcaemia and Stauffer syndrome.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 60-year-old leather tannery worker who smokes has painless visible haematuria. Cystoscopy shows a papillary bladder tumour. What is the most common histological type?
renal-iii/urology.e: Risk factors: smoking, aromatic amines (dye, rubber, leather industries); squamous cell carcinoma is associated with schistosomiasis and chronic catheters. Initial treatment is TURBT.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 15-year-old boy wakes with sudden severe left testicular pain and vomiting. The testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and absent cremasteric reflex. What is the management?
o: Immediate scrotal exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy
renal-iii/urology.e: Testicular salvage falls dramatically after 6 hours; do not delay surgery for imaging if clinical suspicion is high.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 25-year-old sexually active man has gradual-onset scrotal pain and swelling with urethral discharge. Pain is relieved on elevating the testis (positive Prehn's sign). What is the treatment?
o: Ceftriaxone single dose plus doxycycline for 10–14 days
renal-iii/urology.e: Under 35: chlamydia/gonorrhoea; older men: enteric organisms (quinolone). Prehn's sign is unreliable in excluding torsion.

renal-iii/urology.s: A man with a pelvic fracture after a crash has blood at the urethral meatus, a high-riding prostate and cannot void. What should be AVOIDED?
renal-iii/urology.e: Suspected posterior urethral injury (membranous urethra) requires retrograde urethrogram and suprapubic drainage; catheterisation may convert partial to complete tear.

renal-iii/urology.s: A diabetic man has rapidly spreading painful scrotal and perineal swelling with crepitus, blackened skin and sepsis. What is the treatment?
o: Emergency radical surgical debridement with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
renal-iii/urology.e: Fournier gangrene is necrotising fasciitis of the perineum; mortality is high without early debridement.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 40-year-old man has a painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates, and it is possible to get above the swelling. The testis cannot be palpated separately. What is the next step?
o: Scrotal ultrasound to exclude underlying testicular pathology (e.g., tumour)
Aspiration and injection of sclerosant without imaging
renal-iii/urology.e: Secondary hydroceles in adults can be due to tumour, infection or trauma; filarial hydrocele occurs in endemic regions.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 45-year-old man with previous gonococcal urethritis has progressive poor stream and straining. Uroflowmetry shows a flat, plateau-shaped curve. What is the likely diagnosis?
renal-iii/urology.e: Plateau flow pattern suggests stricture; confirmed by retrograde urethrogram; treatment ranges from optical urethrotomy to urethroplasty.

renal-iii/urology.s: A haemodynamically stable patient after blunt trauma has visible haematuria. CT shows a renal laceration >1 cm into the medulla without collecting system injury (grade III). What is the management?
o: Non-operative management with bed rest, serial Hb monitoring and repeat imaging if deterioration
Angioembolisation in all grade III injuries
renal-iii/urology.e: Most blunt renal injuries, even high-grade in stable patients, are managed conservatively; angioembolisation for active bleeding.

renal-iii/urology.s: A 22-year-old man with sickle cell disease has a painful erection lasting 6 hours. Cavernosal blood gas shows hypoxia and acidosis. What is the first-line intervention?
o: Aspiration of corpora cavernosa with intracavernosal phenylephrine
renal-iii/urology.e: Ischaemic (low-flow) priapism >4 hours is a urological emergency to prevent erectile dysfunction.

renal-iii/urology.s: A patient with spina bifida has overflow incontinence with a large post-void residual and recurrent UTIs. What is the best management of bladder emptying?
renal-iii/urology.e: CISC reduces infection risk and protects upper tracts in underactive/dyssynergic bladders.

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A 7-year-old boy has cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema and BP 135/90 mmHg, 2 weeks after impetigo. C3 is low. What is the management?
o: Supportive: salt and fluid restriction, diuretics and antihypertensives; penicillin to eradicate streptococci
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: PSGN usually resolves; C3 normalises within 6–8 weeks (persistently low C3 warrants biopsy for MPGN/C3 glomerulopathy).

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A 4-year-old has generalised oedema, frothy urine, urine protein 4+, albumin 1.5 g/dL, normal BP, no haematuria and normal complement. What is the first-line treatment?
o: Oral prednisolone 60 mg/m²/day for 4–6 weeks then alternate-day tapering, without biopsy
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in 1–10-year-olds is usually steroid-sensitive minimal change disease; biopsy for atypical features or steroid resistance.

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A child with nephrotic syndrome develops fever, abdominal pain and diffuse tenderness with ascites. What is the likely complication?
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: Loss of immunoglobulins and factor B predisposes to encapsulated organism infections; pneumococcal vaccination is recommended.

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old has bloody diarrhoea for 5 days, followed by pallor, oliguria and petechiae. Blood film shows schistocytes; platelets 40 × 10⁹/L; creatinine raised. What is the likely cause?
o: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 (typical HUS)
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: Typical HUS: triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI; supportive care; antibiotics may worsen toxin release.

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-month-old has fever 39°C, poor feeding and vomiting. Catheter urine shows pyuria and E. coli growth. After treatment, which imaging is recommended?
o: Renal and bladder ultrasound (with further imaging such as MCUG/DMSA if atypical or recurrent UTI)
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: Infants <6 months with first febrile UTI need ultrasound; atypical/recurrent infection prompts MCUG and DMSA scan (NICE).

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: MCUG in a 2-year-old with recurrent pyelonephritis shows reflux into a dilated ureter and renal pelvis with blunting of calyces. What is the International Reflux Study grade?
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: I: ureter only; II: pelvis without dilatation; III: mild dilatation; IV: moderate dilatation with calyceal blunting; V: gross tortuosity. Risk of renal scarring increases with grade.

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A 8-year-old boy wets the bed 5 nights a week and has always done so. He is dry during the day and urinalysis is normal. What is the first-line treatment?
o: Enuresis alarm with reassurance and reward systems (desmopressin if rapid short-term control needed)
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: Primary monosymptomatic enuresis: alarm has the best long-term success; desmopressin for short-term (e.g., school trips).

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old has an asymptomatic smooth abdominal mass found by mother while bathing him, not crossing the midline, with hypertension and haematuria. He has aniridia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: WAGR syndrome (Wilms, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, retardation; WT1). Neuroblastoma often crosses the midline, is irregular and calcified, with raised urinary catecholamines.

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: An 18-month-old has an irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline, periorbital bruising ("raccoon eyes") and opsoclonus–myoclonus. Which test supports the diagnosis?
o: Raised urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA)
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest cells in the adrenal medulla; MYCN amplification indicates poor prognosis.

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A child with failure to thrive, polyuria, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, high urinary calcium and normal blood pressure has high renin and aldosterone. What is the diagnosis?
o: Gitelman syndrome with low urinary calcium
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: Bartter mimics loop diuretics (hypercalciuria); Gitelman mimics thiazides (hypocalciuria, hypomagnesaemia); Liddle has hypertension with low renin.

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A 1-year-old with severe dehydration from gastroenteritis has reduced urine output and raised creatinine. After rehydration, urine output recovers and creatinine normalises within 48 hours. What was the type of AKI?
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: Rapid recovery with volume restoration defines prerenal AKI; prolonged hypoperfusion may progress to ATN.

renal-iii/paediatrics.s: A 7-year-old with CKD stage 4 has height below the 3rd centile despite adequate nutrition, corrected acidosis and controlled renal bone disease. What treatment can improve growth?
renal-iii/paediatrics.e: CKD causes GH resistance; rhGH improves final height once metabolic issues are corrected.

renal-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A male neonate has a palpable bladder, poor urinary stream and bilateral hydronephrosis detected antenatally with oligohydramnios. What is the investigation of choice?
renal-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: PUV is the commonest cause of lower urinary tract obstruction in boys; MCUG shows dilated posterior urethra; treat by catheter drainage then endoscopic valve ablation.

renal-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A newborn has a urethral opening on the ventral aspect of the penis near the corona with a dorsal hooded foreskin. What advice is correct?
o: Avoid circumcision because the foreskin is used for repair, planned at 6–18 months
renal-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Hypospadias with bilateral undescended testes warrants evaluation for disorders of sex development.

renal-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A 9-month-old boy has a unilateral impalpable testis on the right. What is the recommended management?
o: Referral for laparoscopic exploration and orchidopexy before 18 months (ideally 6–12 months)
renal-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Early orchidopexy improves fertility and allows surveillance for malignancy; spontaneous descent after 6 months is unlikely.

renal-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A 6-year-old has intermittent loin pain and vomiting after drinking large amounts of fluid. Ultrasound shows a dilated renal pelvis without ureteric dilatation. MAG3 renogram shows obstructive drainage with split function 35%. What is the treatment?
renal-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Pelviureteric junction obstruction with symptoms or declining function (<40%) needs dismembered pyeloplasty.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 45-year-old asymptomatic overweight man has fasting plasma glucose 132 mg/dL and HbA1c 6.8% from the same blood sample. What is the correct interpretation?
o: Diabetes is confirmed because two different tests from the same sample are both above threshold
Diabetes cannot be diagnosed without symptoms
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: ADA: FPG ≥126 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, 2-h OGTT ≥200 mg/dL; two abnormal results (same or separate samples) confirm diagnosis in asymptomatic people.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) on metformin had an MI last year. Which additional drug class is preferred for cardiovascular benefit independent of HbA1c?
o: GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: ADA recommends GLP-1 RA/SGLT2i for established ASCVD, heart failure or CKD; saxagliptin increased HF hospitalisation.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.10, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, ketones 5 mmol/L and K⁺ 3.1 mmol/L. What must be done before starting the insulin infusion?
o: Replace potassium until K⁺ is ≥3.3–3.5 mmol/L while giving IV fluids
Start insulin bolus immediately regardless of K⁺
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Insulin drives K⁺ into cells, causing life-threatening hypokalaemia; fluids first, K⁺ replacement, then fixed-rate insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 70-year-old woman has confusion, glucose 1100 mg/dL, serum osmolality 360 mOsm/kg, pH 7.35 and minimal ketones. What is the priority in management?
o: Gradual IV 0.9% saline rehydration, adding low-dose insulin only once glucose stops falling with fluids
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: HHS: fluid replacement alone lowers glucose; avoid rapid osmolality shifts; thromboprophylaxis because of high VTE risk.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A diabetic man on insulin is found drowsy and unable to swallow. Capillary glucose is 38 mg/dL. What is the immediate treatment?
o: Oral glucose gel between the teeth
IV 10% dextrose 150–200 mL (or IM glucagon 1 mg if no IV access)
IV 50% dextrose rapidly as first choice via a small vein
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: 10% dextrose is preferred (less extravasation injury than 50%); follow with long-acting carbohydrate; glucagon is less effective in alcohol excess/liver disease.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A patient with type 2 diabetes on glimepiride wants to fast during Ramadan. What is the best advice?
o: Pre-Ramadan assessment; reduce dose or switch to a lower-hypoglycaemia agent taken at iftar; break the fast if glucose <70 mg/dL
Fasting is permitted only with insulin
Continue glimepiride at the same dose at suhoor
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: IDF–DAR guidelines: risk stratification; sulfonylureas carry hypoglycaemia risk; SGLT2 inhibitors require attention to hydration.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 30-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, lid lag, proptosis, pretibial myxoedema and a diffuse goitre with bruit. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is high. Which antibody confirms the diagnosis?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Ophthalmopathy and pretibial myxoedema are specific to Graves; uptake scan shows diffuse increased uptake.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A patient on carbimazole develops a sore throat and fever. What is the most important immediate action?
o: Stop carbimazole and check an urgent full blood count for agranulocytosis
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Agranulocytosis occurs in ~0.3%; patients must be warned to report sore throat or fever.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A patient with untreated Graves disease develops fever 40°C, AF at 170/min, agitation and vomiting after an infection. What is the correct sequence of management?
o: Propranolol and propylthiouracil, then iodine (Lugol's) at least 1 hour after PTU, plus hydrocortisone and supportive care
Iodine first, then antithyroid drug after 1 week
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Thionamide before iodine prevents new hormone synthesis from the iodine load; aspirin displaces T4 from binding proteins.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 70-year-old woman with ischaemic heart disease has fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance and TSH 28 mIU/L with low free T4. How should levothyroxine be started?
o: Low dose (12.5–25 micrograms daily) and increase gradually
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Elderly and cardiac patients need slow titration to avoid precipitating angina/arrhythmias; recheck TSH 6–8 weeks after each change.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 35-year-old woman planning pregnancy has TSH 6.2 mIU/L with normal free T4 and positive anti-TPO antibodies. What is recommended?
o: Start levothyroxine, aiming for TSH <2.5 mIU/L before conception
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Treatment is recommended in women planning pregnancy, especially TPO-positive; dose requirement rises ~30% in pregnancy.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A patient with known Addison disease has vomiting, abdominal pain, BP 75/40 mmHg, Na⁺ 124 and K⁺ 6.0 mmol/L. What is the immediate treatment?
o: Wait for cortisol result before treatment
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus and IV 0.9% saline
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Adrenal crisis is life-threatening; never delay treatment for tests. "Sick day rules": double glucocorticoid dose during intercurrent illness.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 40-year-old woman has central obesity, purple striae, proximal myopathy and hypertension. She takes no steroids. What is an appropriate first-line screening test?
o: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (or late-night salivary cortisol or 24-h urinary free cortisol)
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: After confirming hypercortisolism, plasma ACTH separates ACTH-dependent (pituitary/ectopic) from adrenal causes.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 35-year-old has paroxysmal headaches, palpitations, sweating and severe hypertension. Plasma free metanephrines are markedly raised and CT shows a 4 cm adrenal mass. What is the correct preoperative preparation?
o: Alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) first, then beta-blocker, with fluid and salt loading
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Beta-blockade first leaves alpha stimulation unopposed and may cause hypertensive crisis; associations include MEN2, VHL and NF1.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 28-year-old woman has amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Prolactin is 3,200 mIU/L and MRI shows a 7 mm pituitary adenoma. Pregnancy test is negative. What is the first-line treatment?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Dopamine agonists shrink prolactinomas and restore fertility; exclude drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) and hypothyroidism.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 45-year-old man has enlarged hands and feet, coarse facial features, prognathism, sweating and hypertension. IGF-1 is raised. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
o: Oral glucose tolerance test with failure of GH suppression
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Trans-sphenoidal surgery is first-line; complications include cardiomyopathy, colonic polyps, OSA and diabetes.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: After a head injury, a patient passes 8 litres of dilute urine per day with Na⁺ 150 mmol/L. Urine osmolality rises from 150 to 600 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. What is the diagnosis?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Failure to concentrate urine with dehydration but a >50% rise after desmopressin indicates cranial DI.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 55-year-old woman has recurrent renal stones, calcium 11.8 mg/dL, low phosphate and raised PTH. What is the most common cause?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: ~85% are due to a solitary adenoma; localise with sestamibi scan and ultrasound before parathyroidectomy.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: After thyroidectomy, a patient has perioral tingling and carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated above systolic pressure for 3 minutes. What is this sign?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Trousseau's sign is more specific than Chvostek's sign (facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve).

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A 40-year-old woman has BMI 36 kg/m² with prediabetes despite lifestyle measures. Which pharmacological option achieves the greatest weight loss?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: GLP-1 RA and dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists produce ~15–20% weight loss; thyroxine for weight loss is inappropriate.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A diabetic patient with peripheral neuropathy has a painless ulcer under the first metatarsal head. The probe-to-bone test is positive. What complication is most likely?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Confirm with X-ray/MRI and bone biopsy/culture; offloading and multidisciplinary foot care are essential.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: When should retinal screening start in a patient newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes?
o: At the time of diagnosis, then every 1–2 years
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Type 2 diabetics may already have retinopathy at diagnosis; in type 1, screening starts 5 years after diagnosis.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A patient in ICU with septic shock has low T3, low-normal T4 and normal TSH. What is the appropriate management?
o: No thyroid hormone treatment; repeat thyroid tests after recovery
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Non-thyroidal illness syndrome is adaptive; replacement is not beneficial.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A newly diagnosed adult with type 1 diabetes is started on insulin. Which regimen best mimics physiological insulin secretion?
o: Basal–bolus: once-daily long-acting analogue plus rapid-acting insulin with meals
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Basal–bolus or insulin pump with carbohydrate counting gives the best flexibility and control.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.s: A patient with squamous cell lung cancer has calcium 14 mg/dL with suppressed PTH. What is the most likely mechanism?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/medicine.e: Humoral hypercalcaemia is commonest; others include osteolytic metastases and calcitriol production by lymphoma.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: A 40-year-old woman has a solitary 2.5 cm thyroid nodule with normal TSH. Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic solid nodule with microcalcifications. What is the next step?
o: Observation with repeat TSH in 1 year
Ultrasound-guided FNAC reported using the Bethesda system
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.e: Suspicious ultrasound features (TI-RADS) warrant FNA; a low TSH prompts an isotope scan (hot nodules are rarely malignant).

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: FNAC of a thyroid nodule shows cells with "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei, nuclear grooves and psammoma bodies. What is the diagnosis?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.e: Commonest thyroid cancer; lymphatic spread; associated with radiation and BRAF mutation; excellent prognosis.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: A 30-year-old with a thyroid mass has raised serum calcitonin. His father had a phaeochromocytoma. What must be excluded before thyroidectomy?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.e: MEN2A: medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism; operating with an undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma risks hypertensive crisis.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: Why can FNAC not distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma?
o: Carcinoma requires capsular or vascular invasion, which is seen only on histology
Follicular cells are never obtained on FNAC
Adenomas are always hot on scan
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.e: Follicular neoplasms (Bethesda IV) need diagnostic hemithyroidectomy; follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously to bone and lung.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: Four hours after total thyroidectomy, a patient develops stridor, rapidly enlarging neck swelling and respiratory distress. What is the immediate action?
o: Open the wound at the bedside (skin and strap muscle sutures) to evacuate the haematoma
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.e: Tension haematoma compresses the airway; evacuate immediately (SCOOP), then return to theatre.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: After total thyroidectomy, a patient has stridor on extubation with both vocal cords fixed in the paramedian position. What is the cause?
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.e: Bilateral RLN injury may need reintubation or tracheostomy; unilateral injury causes hoarseness; external branch of superior laryngeal nerve injury affects voice pitch.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: A 42-year-old woman has a 2 cm hard, irregular, painless lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. What is the standard evaluation?
o: Clinical examination, imaging (mammography plus ultrasound) and core needle biopsy
Excision biopsy as the first step
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.e: Triple assessment is the standard for any breast lump; ultrasound is first-line under 35 years.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: A 20-year-old woman has a 2 cm smooth, firm, highly mobile, painless breast lump. Ultrasound and core biopsy confirm fibroadenoma. What is the management?
o: Reassurance; excision only if enlarging, >3–4 cm or at the patient's request
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.e: Rapidly growing or giant lesions are excised to exclude phyllodes tumour.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: A breastfeeding mother at 4 weeks postpartum has a painful, red, fluctuant 3 cm breast swelling with fever. What is the management?
o: Ultrasound-guided aspiration (repeated if needed) with flucloxacillin, continuing breastfeeding or expressing
Stop breastfeeding and bind the breasts
endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.e: S. aureus is the usual cause; incision and drainage if aspiration fails or skin is necrotic.

endocrine-and-reproduction-iii/surgery.s: A postmenopausal woman has breast cancer that is ER-positive, PR-positive and HER2-negative. Which adjuvant endocrine therapy is preferred?
