neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A 6-month-old has clusters of sudden flexion of the neck, trunk and limbs on waking, with developmental regression. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. What is the first-line treatment?
o: Vigabatrin (especially with tuberous sclerosis) or ACTH/prednisolone
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: West syndrome: spasms, hypsarrhythmia and developmental arrest; early treatment improves outcome; examine skin for ash-leaf macules.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A 7-year-old has frequent brief episodes of staring with eyelid flutter, lasting 10 seconds, provoked by hyperventilation. EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave. What is the drug of choice?
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence seizures; valproate and lamotrigine are alternatives.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old born at 28 weeks has delayed motor milestones, scissoring of the legs, increased tone, brisk reflexes and toe walking; the condition is non-progressive. What is the diagnosis?
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: CP is a non-progressive motor disorder from an early brain insult; periventricular leukomalacia is typical in preterms; multidisciplinary management.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: By what age should a child normally be able to walk unsupported, with referral warranted if not achieved?
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Red flags: no social smile by 8 weeks, not sitting unsupported by 9 months, no walking by 18 months, no words by 18 months, hand preference before 12 months.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old has poor eye contact, absent pointing, no pretend play, repetitive lining up of toys and distress at routine change. What is the most appropriate step?
o: Refer for multidisciplinary developmental assessment including hearing test
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Early behavioural intervention improves outcomes; medication only for severe irritability/aggression.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A 8-year-old boy has inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity for 2 years, present both at home and at school, impairing learning. What is the first-line management in school-age children?
o: Parent training/behavioural programme, with methylphenidate if symptoms persist and are severe
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Monitor growth, appetite, sleep, BP and pulse on stimulants; symptoms must occur in ≥2 settings for at least 6 months.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A 7-year-old has 7 café-au-lait macules >5 mm, axillary freckling and Lisch nodules. What is the mode of inheritance?
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Complications: optic glioma, scoliosis, hypertension (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma), learning difficulties. NF2 (chromosome 22): bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A child with infantile spasms has hypopigmented "ash-leaf" macules, a shagreen patch and facial angiofibromas. Which finding on imaging is expected?
o: Cortical tubers and subependymal nodules on brain MRI
Basal ganglia calcification with band keratopathy
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2): also cardiac rhabdomyoma and renal angiomyolipoma; everolimus is used for SEGA.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A healthy 18-month-old cries after being scolded, holds his breath, turns blue and briefly loses consciousness, then recovers within a minute. Examination and ECG are normal. What is the management?
o: EEG and CT brain in all
Reassurance and parental education; check for iron deficiency
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Cyanotic breath-holding spells are benign and resolve by 4–5 years; iron supplementation reduces frequency in anaemic children.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old has sudden asymmetric flaccid weakness of one leg with fever and preserved sensation. What is the immediate public health action in Pakistan?
o: Notify as acute flaccid paralysis and collect two stool samples 24 hours apart for poliovirus
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: All AFP cases under 15 years must be notified and investigated; Pakistan remains polio-endemic, so surveillance is critical.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A term baby born after a difficult delivery has Apgar 3 at 5 minutes, cord pH 6.9, seizures and hypotonia at 4 hours of age. What intervention improves neurodevelopmental outcome?
o: Therapeutic hypothermia started within 6 hours for moderate–severe HIE
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Cooling to 33.5°C for 72 hours reduces death and disability in settings with intensive care support.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-day-old has repetitive lip smacking, cycling movements and apnoea. What is the most important immediate investigation?
o: Blood glucose (with calcium, electrolytes and sepsis screen)
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, sepsis/meningitis and HIE are common causes; phenobarbital remains the usual first-line anticonvulsant.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A term neonate with severe untreated jaundice develops lethargy, poor feeding, retrocollis and opisthotonus. Which long-term sequelae are typical?
o: Choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss and upward gaze palsy
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Unconjugated bilirubin deposits in the basal ganglia; prevention by phototherapy/exchange transfusion at appropriate thresholds.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: Which organisms most commonly cause bacterial meningitis in children aged over 3 months?
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria. Hib has declined with vaccination; empirical ceftriaxone ± vancomycin.

neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.s: A 6-year-old has morning headaches with vomiting, ataxia and papilloedema. MRI shows a midline cerebellar tumour with hydrocephalus. What is the most likely tumour?
neurosciences-iii/paediatrics.e: Medulloblastoma is the commonest malignant posterior fossa tumour in children; may seed through CSF; treated with surgery, craniospinal radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.s: A 20-year-old struck on the temple had brief loss of consciousness, then talked normally, and 2 hours later becomes drowsy with a dilated right pupil. What does CT show?
o: Diffuse blood in sulci and cisterns
Biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense collection not crossing suture lines
Multiple petechial haemorrhages at grey–white junction
neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.e: Extradural haematoma is usually from a middle meningeal artery tear with a temporal bone fracture; urgent craniotomy and evacuation.

neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.s: An 80-year-old on aspirin has progressive confusion and headache 4 weeks after a minor fall. CT shows a crescentic hypodense collection over the right hemisphere with midline shift. What is the treatment?
neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.e: Bridging vein rupture in elderly/alcoholic patients; middle meningeal artery embolisation is an emerging adjunct.

neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.s: A head-injured patient opens eyes to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds and withdraws from painful stimulus. What is the GCS?
neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.e: E2 + V2 + M4 = 8; GCS ≤8 indicates the need for definitive airway protection.

neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.s: A head-injured patient develops hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. What does this triad indicate?
o: Cushing reflex due to critically raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation
neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.e: Management: head elevation 30°, normocapnia, sedation, mannitol/hypertonic saline, treat cause; keep cerebral perfusion pressure >60 mmHg.

neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.s: A patient after head trauma has clear fluid dripping from the nose, periorbital bruising and a "halo" sign on the pillow. What is the appropriate management?
o: Avoid nasogastric tube and nasal packing; most CSF leaks close spontaneously with conservative management
Insert a nasogastric tube for feeding
neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.e: CSF confirmed by beta-2 transferrin; prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely recommended; persistent leaks need repair.

neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.s: A patient after a high-speed collision is deeply unconscious (GCS 5) with a near-normal CT. MRI shows multiple small haemorrhages at the grey–white matter junction and corpus callosum. What is the diagnosis?
neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.e: DAI results from rotational/shearing forces; management is supportive with ICP control; prognosis is often poor.

neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.s: A 55-year-old woman has seizures and progressive leg weakness. MRI shows an extra-axial, dural-based, homogeneously enhancing mass with a dural tail over the parasagittal region. What is the likely tumour?
neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.e: Meningiomas are usually benign (WHO grade 1); surgery is curative when completely resected; observation for small asymptomatic lesions.

neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.s: A patient with a known pituitary macroadenoma develops sudden severe headache, vomiting, bitemporal visual loss and ophthalmoplegia. What is the essential immediate treatment?
o: IV hydrocortisone and urgent neurosurgical/endocrine assessment
neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.e: Pituitary apoplexy causes acute adrenal insufficiency; urgent MRI and surgical decompression if vision is threatened.

neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.s: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media has fever, headache and a new hemiparesis. CT shows a ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema in the temporal lobe. What is the management?
o: Aspiration/excision with prolonged IV antibiotics and treatment of the primary source
neurosciences-iii/neurosurgery.e: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with a mass lesion; anaerobes and streptococci are common organisms.

neurosciences-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A newborn has a lumbosacral sac containing neural tissue with leaking CSF, lower limb weakness and a patulous anus. What is the immediate management?
o: Apply povidone-iodine directly to neural tissue
Cover the defect with sterile saline-soaked gauze, nurse prone, give antibiotics and arrange surgical closure within 24–48 hours
Immediate shunt insertion before closure in all
neurosciences-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Monitor head circumference for hydrocephalus (Chiari II); prevention is periconceptional folic acid.

neurosciences-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A 3-year-old with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt has headache, vomiting, drowsiness and a bulging fontanelle-like tense shunt reservoir. What is the most likely problem?
o: Shunt obstruction with raised intracranial pressure
neurosciences-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Shunt malfunction or infection is an emergency; CT/shunt series and neurosurgical review are required.

neurosciences-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A 4-month-old has a long narrow head with a ridge along the sagittal suture and normal development. What is the diagnosis?
o: Scaphocephaly due to premature fusion of the sagittal suture
neurosciences-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Sagittal synostosis is the commonest single-suture craniosynostosis; surgery is done for cosmesis and to prevent raised ICP in multi-suture disease.

neurosciences-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A 4-year-old fell from a bed and vomited twice but is alert (GCS 15) with a boggy occipital swelling. Which finding would mandate an urgent CT head?
o: Suspicion of a skull fracture (boggy swelling), GCS <15, focal neurology, seizure or ≥3 episodes of vomiting
Crying at the time of injury
neurosciences-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: NICE paediatric criteria; minimise radiation with observation when criteria are not met.

neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.s: A 60-year-old has clumsy hands, difficulty with buttons, unsteady gait, brisk lower limb reflexes and extensor plantars with neck pain. What is the diagnosis and management?
o: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy; MRI cervical spine and surgical decompression
neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.e: Progressive myelopathy needs early decompression; Lhermitte's sign and Hoffman's sign may be present.

neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.s: A 68-year-old has bilateral leg pain and heaviness on walking that is relieved by sitting or leaning forward, with normal peripheral pulses. What is the diagnosis?
o: Neurogenic claudication due to lumbar canal stenosis
neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.e: Relief with flexion ("shopping trolley sign") and preserved pulses distinguish it from vascular claudication; MRI confirms.

neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.s: A macrosomic newborn after shoulder dystocia holds the right arm adducted and internally rotated with the forearm pronated ("waiter's tip"). Which nerve roots are injured?
o: C4 and C5 with phrenic palsy in all
neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.e: Erb's palsy (upper trunk); Klumpke's palsy (C8–T1) causes a claw hand with Horner syndrome; most recover with physiotherapy.

neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.s: A patient with a fracture at the medial epicondyle has clawing of the ring and little fingers and cannot adduct the thumb; Froment's sign is positive. Which nerve is injured?
neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.e: Froment's sign indicates weak adductor pollicis; "ulnar paradox" — higher lesions cause less clawing.

neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.s: A patient develops foot drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot after prolonged squatting or a tight plaster below the knee. Which nerve is compressed?
o: Common peroneal nerve at the neck of the fibula
neurosciences-iii/orthopaedics.e: Inversion is preserved (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve), distinguishing it from an L5 root lesion; ankle-foot orthosis and removal of the cause.

git-iii/medicine.s: A 55-year-old with 10 years of heartburn has endoscopy showing salmon-coloured mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction; biopsy shows intestinal metaplasia without dysplasia. What is the management?
o: Radiofrequency ablation for non-dysplastic short segments in all patients
Long-term proton pump inhibitor with endoscopic surveillance every 2–5 years
git-iii/medicine.e: Barrett oesophagus predisposes to adenocarcinoma; ablation is indicated for dysplasia.

git-iii/medicine.s: A 40-year-old with a duodenal ulcer tests positive for H. pylori (no penicillin allergy). What is an appropriate first-line regimen?
o: PPI with amoxicillin and clarithromycin (or metronidazole) for 14 days, or bismuth quadruple therapy
git-iii/medicine.e: Confirm eradication with urea breath test/stool antigen 4 weeks after therapy, off PPI for 2 weeks.

git-iii/medicine.s: A 60-year-old presents with haematemesis. Which score is used before endoscopy to decide whether he needs admission and intervention?
git-iii/medicine.e: Glasgow–Blatchford 0–1 may allow outpatient management; full Rockall score is calculated post-endoscopy.

git-iii/medicine.s: A cirrhotic patient has massive haematemesis with BP 85/50 mmHg. After resuscitation, which drug should be started before endoscopy?
git-iii/medicine.e: Band ligation within 12 hours; antibiotics reduce mortality; propranolol is used for secondary prophylaxis, not acute bleeding.

git-iii/medicine.s: A 25-year-old woman has chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, iron deficiency anaemia and an itchy vesicular rash on the elbows. Which test should be done first (while on a gluten-containing diet)?
o: Serum IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA
git-iii/medicine.e: Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia; treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet.

git-iii/medicine.s: A patient with ulcerative colitis passes 8 bloody stools/day with temperature 38.2°C, pulse 105/min, Hb 9.5 g/dL and ESR 45 mm/h. According to Truelove and Witts criteria, how is this classified and treated?
o: Severe colitis; admit for IV hydrocortisone, VTE prophylaxis and daily review
Severe; immediate colectomy without medical therapy
git-iii/medicine.e: If no response by day 3, consider rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin, with surgical review. Avoid antimotility drugs (toxic megacolon risk).

git-iii/medicine.s: Which feature favours Crohn disease over ulcerative colitis?
o: Transmural inflammation with skip lesions and perianal fistulae
git-iii/medicine.e: Crohn: mouth to anus, non-caseating granulomas, strictures and fistulae; smoking worsens Crohn but is "protective" in UC.

git-iii/medicine.s: Before starting azathioprine for inflammatory bowel disease, which test should be checked?
git-iii/medicine.e: Low TPMT increases myelosuppression risk; monitor FBC and LFTs; avoid allopurinol co-prescription without dose reduction.

git-iii/medicine.s: A 28-year-old has 8 months of abdominal pain relieved by defecation with alternating bowel habit, bloating, normal examination, normal CBC, CRP, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin. What is the diagnosis?
git-iii/medicine.e: Rome IV criteria; management: dietary modification (low FODMAP), antispasmodics, laxatives/loperamide, low-dose TCA and psychological therapies.

git-iii/medicine.s: A patient develops profuse watery diarrhoea 1 week after ceftriaxone. Stool is positive for C. difficile toxin. What is first-line treatment?
o: Oral metronidazole as preferred first line
git-iii/medicine.e: Stop the precipitating antibiotic; recurrent disease may need fidaxomicin or faecal microbiota transplantation; isolate the patient.

git-iii/medicine.s: A cirrhotic patient with ascites has abdominal pain and fever. Ascitic fluid shows 600 neutrophils/mm³. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
o: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; IV cefotaxime plus albumin
git-iii/medicine.e: SBP: ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm³; albumin reduces hepatorenal syndrome; secondary prophylaxis with norfloxacin/ciprofloxacin.

git-iii/medicine.s: A cirrhotic patient becomes confused with asterixis after an upper GI bleed. What is the first-line treatment?
o: Lactulose (titrated to 2–3 soft stools/day) with treatment of the precipitant, adding rifaximin if needed
git-iii/medicine.e: Precipitants: GI bleed, infection, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, dehydration. Protein restriction is no longer recommended.

git-iii/medicine.s: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites has creatinine rising to 2.5 mg/dL with bland urinary sediment, urine Na⁺ <10 mmol/L and no improvement after stopping diuretics and giving albumin. What is the treatment?
o: Terlipressin with albumin, and assessment for liver transplantation
git-iii/medicine.e: HRS-AKI is a functional renal failure from splanchnic vasodilatation; transplantation is definitive.

git-iii/medicine.s: A 45-year-old with chronic hepatitis C genotype 3 and compensated cirrhosis asks about treatment. What is current standard therapy?
o: Pegylated interferon plus ribavirin for 48 weeks
Direct-acting antiviral combination (e.g., sofosbuvir–velpatasvir) for 12 weeks
git-iii/medicine.e: DAAs achieve sustained virological response >95%; Pakistan has one of the world's highest HCV burdens and a national elimination programme.

git-iii/medicine.s: Which patient with chronic hepatitis B most clearly needs antiviral therapy?
o: HBeAg-positive with HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL and ALT more than twice normal
Inactive carrier with normal ALT and HBV DNA <2,000 IU/mL
Isolated anti-HBc positive with undetectable DNA
git-iii/medicine.e: Tenofovir or entecavir are first-line; all cirrhotic patients with detectable DNA need treatment; screen for hepatocellular carcinoma with 6-monthly ultrasound.

git-iii/medicine.s: A patient with heavy alcohol use has jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, AST 180 U/L, ALT 70 U/L, bilirubin 15 mg/dL and prolonged PT. Maddrey discriminant function is 48. What treatment may be considered?
o: Liver biopsy before any treatment in all
Prednisolone (after excluding infection/GI bleeding) plus nutrition and abstinence
git-iii/medicine.e: AST:ALT ratio >2 suggests alcoholic liver disease; steroids are considered when DF ≥32; no benefit if infection or renal failure.

git-iii/medicine.s: A 35-year-old man has fever, right upper quadrant pain and tender hepatomegaly. Ultrasound shows a single large right lobe abscess with "anchovy sauce" aspirate. What is the treatment?
o: Metronidazole followed by a luminal amoebicide (e.g., paromomycin or diloxanide furoate)
Surgical resection of the liver segment
git-iii/medicine.e: Aspiration is needed for large left-lobe abscesses, impending rupture or no response after 72 hours; luminal agents clear intestinal cysts.

git-iii/medicine.s: A 40-year-old has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids with regurgitation. Barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus with a smooth "bird beak" narrowing. What confirms the diagnosis?
o: High-resolution oesophageal manometry showing failed relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter with aplastic peristalsis
git-iii/medicine.e: Endoscopy is still required to exclude pseudoachalasia (malignancy); treat with pneumatic dilatation, POEM or Heller myotomy.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 22-year-old man has periumbilical pain shifting to the right iliac fossa with anorexia, vomiting, low-grade fever and tenderness at McBurney's point with guarding. What is the management?
o: Observation with analgesia alone for 48 hours
git-iii/surgery.e: Alvarado score aids diagnosis; ultrasound/CT help in equivocal cases, especially in women and children.

git-iii/surgery.s: A patient presents on day 6 with a tender right iliac fossa mass, no peritonitis and settled fever. CT confirms an appendicular phlegmon without abscess. What is the initial management?
o: Conservative (Ochsner–Sherren) regimen with IV antibiotics and observation, with interval imaging/appendicectomy as indicated
git-iii/surgery.e: Failure to settle or abscess formation requires drainage; colonic imaging is advised in older patients to exclude malignancy.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 50-year-old NSAID user has sudden severe epigastric pain with board-like rigidity. Erect chest X-ray shows free gas under the diaphragm. What is the treatment?
o: Resuscitation, IV antibiotics, nasogastric decompression and emergency laparotomy with omental (Graham) patch repair
Conservative management with PPI in all patients
git-iii/surgery.e: Test and treat H. pylori postoperatively; laparoscopic repair is an option in stable patients.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 60-year-old with previous appendicectomy has colicky central abdominal pain, vomiting, absolute constipation and distension. X-ray shows multiple dilated central loops with valvulae conniventes. What is the commonest cause?
git-iii/surgery.e: Initial management: drip and suck (NG tube, IV fluids), with surgery for strangulation, closed loop or failure to settle.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 70-year-old woman has a tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with vomiting and distension. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
git-iii/surgery.e: Femoral hernias are commoner in women and have the highest strangulation risk; inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the pubic tubercle.

git-iii/surgery.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes an indirect from a direct inguinal hernia?
o: An indirect hernia passes through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and may reach the scrotum
A direct hernia passes through the deep ring
A direct hernia commonly descends into the scrotum
An indirect hernia is medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
Indirect hernias occur only in the elderly
git-iii/surgery.e: Direct hernias bulge through Hesselbach's triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels; indirect hernias are commoner and more often strangulate.

git-iii/surgery.s: An elderly constipated man has massive abdominal distension with a "coffee bean" sign on X-ray arising from the left iliac fossa. There are no peritoneal signs. What is the initial management?
o: Endoscopic (flexible sigmoidoscopy) decompression with flatus tube insertion
git-iii/surgery.e: Recurrence is common — elective sigmoid colectomy is considered; peritonitis or failed decompression requires surgery.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 45-year-old obese woman has right upper quadrant pain for 2 days, fever, and a positive Murphy's sign. Ultrasound shows gallstones with a thick-walled gallbladder and pericholecystic fluid. What is the preferred management?
o: Elective surgery after 3 months in all
Antibiotics with early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (ideally within 7 days of onset)
git-iii/surgery.e: Early cholecystectomy reduces recurrence and complications; cholecystostomy for unfit patients.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 65-year-old has fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain (Charcot's triad), with hypotension and confusion. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with stones. What is the definitive treatment?
o: Urgent biliary decompression by ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction after resuscitation and antibiotics
Percutaneous drainage of the gallbladder only
git-iii/surgery.e: Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and confusion (suppurative cholangitis); biliary drainage is life-saving.

git-iii/surgery.s: An elderly woman has small bowel obstruction with pneumobilia and an ectopic gallstone in the right iliac fossa on CT. What is the underlying mechanism?
o: Cholecystoduodenal fistula allowing a large stone to obstruct the terminal ileum
git-iii/surgery.e: Rigler's triad: pneumobilia, small bowel obstruction and an ectopic gallstone; treatment is enterolithotomy.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 65-year-old has painless progressive jaundice, weight loss and a palpable non-tender gallbladder. What does Courvoisier's law suggest?
o: The cause is unlikely to be gallstones — suspect periampullary/pancreatic head malignancy
git-iii/surgery.e: Investigate with ultrasound, CT pancreas protocol, CA 19-9 and EUS/ERCP; Whipple's procedure for resectable disease.

git-iii/surgery.s: What are the two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis worldwide?
git-iii/surgery.e: "I GET SMASHED" mnemonic; ultrasound and lipase/amylase confirm; LFTs help identify a biliary cause.

git-iii/surgery.s: A patient with severe acute pancreatitis has persistent organ failure at 72 hours. What is the correct nutritional approach?
o: Keep nil by mouth for 2 weeks
Early enteral nutrition (nasogastric or nasojejunal) rather than nil by mouth
git-iii/surgery.e: Enteral feeding maintains gut barrier function and reduces infection; prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely recommended.

git-iii/surgery.s: Six weeks after acute pancreatitis, a patient has persistent epigastric pain, early satiety and a 9 cm fluid collection with a mature wall on CT. What is the treatment of choice?
git-iii/surgery.e: Asymptomatic pseudocysts may be observed; drainage for symptoms, infection or complications after wall maturation (>4–6 weeks).

git-iii/surgery.s: A 65-year-old has iron deficiency anaemia, weight loss and a right iliac fossa mass. What is the likely site of the tumour?
git-iii/surgery.e: Right-sided tumours present with anaemia and mass; left-sided with obstruction and altered bowel habit; rectal with bleeding and tenesmus.

git-iii/surgery.s: A colonic tumour invades through the muscularis propria into the subserosa with 3 positive regional lymph nodes and no distant metastasis. What is the TNM stage?
git-iii/surgery.e: Stage III (node-positive) disease requires adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX) after resection.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 20-year-old with hundreds of colonic adenomas has a family history of colon cancer at a young age. What is the underlying mutation and management?
o: APC gene mutation; prophylactic total colectomy
git-iii/surgery.e: FAP has near 100% cancer risk by age 40; Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair genes) needs intensive surveillance.

git-iii/surgery.s: A patient has bright red painless rectal bleeding with prolapse during defecation that reduces spontaneously. What grade of haemorrhoids is this and what is initial treatment?
o: Grade 2; dietary fibre, fluids and rubber band ligation
git-iii/surgery.e: Grade 1: no prolapse; 2: prolapse with spontaneous reduction; 3: needs manual reduction; 4: irreducible. Always exclude proximal pathology in older patients.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 30-year-old has severe pain during and after defecation with streaks of fresh blood on the toilet paper. A posterior midline tear is visible. What is first-line treatment?
o: Stool softeners, high fibre, sitz baths and topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem
git-iii/surgery.e: Chronic fissures may need botulinum toxin or lateral sphincterotomy (risk of incontinence); lateral fissures suggest Crohn, TB or malignancy.

git-iii/surgery.s: A patient has recurrent perianal discharge with an external opening 2 cm from the anal verge posteriorly. According to Goodsall's rule, where does the internal opening lie?
o: At the dentate line anteriorly in a straight line
In the posterior midline, reached by a curved tract
git-iii/surgery.e: Anterior openings track radially (straight); posterior openings curve to the posterior midline. MRI defines complex fistulae; treatment depends on sphincter involvement.

git-iii/surgery.s: A diabetic man has severe perianal pain with a tender, fluctuant, red swelling and fever. What is the management?
o: Sitz baths and review in 1 week
git-iii/surgery.e: Delayed drainage risks extension and Fournier gangrene; look for underlying Crohn disease in recurrent cases.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 60-year-old has left iliac fossa pain, fever and raised CRP. CT shows sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic inflammation but no abscess or perforation (Hinchey Ia). What is the management?
o: Antibiotics (or even observation in selected uncomplicated cases), bowel rest and analgesia
git-iii/surgery.e: Colonoscopy is deferred 6–8 weeks to exclude malignancy; Hinchey III/IV (purulent/faecal peritonitis) needs surgery.

git-iii/surgery.s: An 80-year-old with atrial fibrillation has sudden severe central abdominal pain with minimal tenderness on examination, and raised lactate with metabolic acidosis. What is the diagnosis?
o: Acute mesenteric ischaemia due to superior mesenteric artery embolism
git-iii/surgery.e: "Pain out of proportion to signs"; CT angiography is diagnostic; treatment is embolectomy/revascularisation and resection of necrotic bowel.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 60-year-old smoker with progressive dysphagia to solids and weight loss has a mid-oesophageal irregular stricture. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. Which investigation best assesses local T staging?
git-iii/surgery.e: CT and PET-CT assess distant spread; adenocarcinoma is commoner in the lower third (Barrett), squamous in the upper two-thirds.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 65-year-old with weight loss and epigastric pain has a hard left supraclavicular lymph node. What is this sign called?
git-iii/surgery.e: Gastric cancer spreads to Virchow's node, umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph), ovaries (Krukenberg) and pelvic peritoneum (Blumer's shelf).

git-iii/surgery.s: A 28-year-old woman has chronic abdominal pain, low-grade fever, weight loss and ascites. Ascitic fluid shows lymphocytes with high protein and ADA 60 U/L; CT shows thickened ileocaecal region and matted mesenteric nodes. What is the management?
o: Antituberculous therapy for at least 6 months
git-iii/surgery.e: Abdominal TB mimics Crohn disease; surgery is reserved for obstruction, perforation or failure of medical therapy.

git-iii/surgery.s: A 40-year-old sheep farmer has a cystic liver lesion with daughter cysts and calcified wall. What is the treatment?
o: Albendazole with PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, re-aspiration) or surgery with precautions against spillage
git-iii/surgery.e: Spillage can cause anaphylaxis and secondary hydatidosis; scolicidal agents and careful technique are essential.

git-iii/surgery.s: A hypotensive patient after a road accident has a positive FAST scan with free fluid in Morrison's pouch and remains unstable after 2 L of fluid. What is the management?
git-iii/surgery.e: Unstable patients with positive FAST go to theatre; stable patients may have CT and non-operative management of solid organ injuries.

git-iii/surgery.s: A stable 25-year-old with a grade II splenic laceration is managed non-operatively. What advice is essential if splenectomy becomes necessary?
o: Vaccination against encapsulated organisms and antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent overwhelming post-splenectomy infection
git-iii/surgery.e: Pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal and annual influenza vaccines, plus penicillin prophylaxis and a medical alert card.

git-iii/surgery.s: Endoscopy in a patient with melaena shows a duodenal ulcer with a visible non-bleeding vessel (Forrest IIa). What is the management?
o: Endoscopic therapy (e.g., adrenaline injection plus thermal/clip) with high-dose IV PPI infusion
git-iii/surgery.e: High-risk stigmata (Forrest I–IIb) require endoscopic haemostasis; test for H. pylori and stop NSAIDs.

git-iii/surgery.s: On day 5 after an anterior resection, a patient has fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain and feculent fluid in the drain. What is the immediate management?
o: Resuscitation, IV antibiotics, CT with contrast and surgical re-exploration/diversion
git-iii/surgery.e: Anastomotic leak is a major cause of postoperative mortality; early recognition and source control are vital.

git-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A 5-week-old firstborn boy has non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds and remains hungry. He is dehydrated with a palpable olive-shaped mass. What biochemical abnormality is expected?
git-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Correct fluids and electrolytes before Ramstedt pyloromyotomy — surgery is never an emergency.

git-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A 9-month-old has episodic inconsolable crying with drawing up of legs, vomiting and "redcurrant jelly" stool. A sausage-shaped mass is felt in the right upper quadrant. What is the first-line treatment in a stable child?
o: Pneumatic (air) or hydrostatic reduction under imaging guidance
git-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Contraindications to reduction: peritonitis, perforation, shock. Ileocolic intussusception usually follows viral illness/lymphoid hyperplasia.

git-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A term neonate fails to pass meconium in the first 48 hours and has abdominal distension with explosive stool after rectal examination. What is the diagnostic test?
o: Rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve trunks
git-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Aganglionosis of the distal bowel; risk of enterocolitis; treated with pull-through surgery.

git-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A 3-week-old has sudden bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. Upper GI contrast shows the duodenojejunal flexure to the right of the midline with a "corkscrew" appearance. What is the management?
git-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is midgut volvulus until proven otherwise — delay causes bowel necrosis.

git-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A 10-day-old preterm formula-fed infant has abdominal distension, bloody stools and bilious aspirates. X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis. What is the initial management?
o: Stop feeds, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics with serial X-rays
git-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Surgery for perforation (pneumoperitoneum) or deterioration; breast milk reduces risk.

git-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A newborn with Down syndrome has bilious vomiting on day 1. X-ray shows a "double bubble" with no distal gas. What is the diagnosis?
git-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Associated with trisomy 21 and polyhydramnios; treated by duodenoduodenostomy after fluid resuscitation.

git-iii/paediatric-surgery.s: A newborn boy has no anal opening and meconium is seen at the tip of the penis. What does this indicate?
o: High anorectal malformation with rectourethral fistula requiring colostomy and later definitive repair
Low malformation treatable by simple anoplasty
git-iii/paediatric-surgery.e: Assess for VACTERL associations; invertogram/perineal ultrasound helps define the level.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old with diarrhoea has sunken eyes, drinks eagerly and has slow skin pinch, but is not lethargic. According to IMCI, what is the classification and treatment?
o: Some dehydration; ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours (Plan B) with continued feeding
No dehydration; Plan A at home only
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Zinc 20 mg daily for 10–14 days (10 mg if <6 months); antibiotics only for dysentery, cholera or systemic infection.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 1-year-old (10 kg) is lethargic, unable to drink, with very slow skin pinch and sunken eyes. What is the correct IV fluid plan?
o: Ringer's lactate 100 mL/kg: 30 mL/kg in the first hour, then 70 mL/kg over 5 hours
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Infants <12 months: 30 mL/kg over 1 hour then 70 mL/kg over 5 hours; children ≥12 months: 30 mL/kg over 30 min then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours. Reassess frequently.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 4-year-old has bloody diarrhoea with fever and abdominal cramps. What is the recommended treatment according to WHO?
o: Oral ciprofloxacin (or azithromycin) for shigellosis with ORS and zinc
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Shigella is the commonest cause of bloody diarrhoea; antimotility drugs are contraindicated; watch for HUS with E. coli O157.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 15-month-old has had diarrhoea for 20 days with weight loss. Stool examination is negative for parasites. What is the most appropriate dietary management?
o: Reduce lactose load (continue breastfeeding), give frequent energy-dense feeds, micronutrients including zinc, and treat infections
Give only clear fluids for 1 week
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Persistent diarrhoea (≥14 days) needs nutritional rehabilitation and evaluation for infection (including HIV, TB) and micronutrient deficiency.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old with bilateral pitting oedema, MUAC 10.5 cm and poor appetite is admitted. Which feed is used in the stabilisation phase?
o: F-75 therapeutic milk with cautious feeding, treating hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and infection
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Rapid refeeding causes refeeding syndrome/heart failure; ReSoMal is used for dehydration; F-100/RUTF in the rehabilitation phase.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 4-year-old passes hard stools twice a week with painful defecation, stool withholding and occasional soiling. Examination is normal with a normal spine and anal position. What is the first-line management?
o: Disimpaction and maintenance with polyethylene glycol (osmotic laxative), toilet training and dietary advice
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Red flags for organic disease: delayed meconium, ribbon stools, failure to thrive, abnormal neurology, anal abnormality.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A thriving 3-month-old posset milk after most feeds without distress, weight gain is normal and examination is unremarkable. What is the management?
o: Reassurance, smaller more frequent feeds and upright positioning after feeds
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Physiological reflux resolves by 12–18 months; investigate if faltering growth, haematemesis, chronic cough or apnoea.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 6-week-old formula-fed infant has blood-streaked loose stools, eczema and vomiting, but is otherwise well. What is the management?
o: Extensively hydrolysed formula trial (or maternal dairy exclusion if breastfed)
Soy formula for all infants under 6 months
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Non-IgE-mediated CMPA responds to elimination and recurrence on challenge; most children outgrow it by 3 years.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 6-week-old has persistent jaundice with pale stools, dark urine and conjugated bilirubin of 6 mg/dL. What is the essential next step?
o: Urgent referral for investigation and Kasai portoenterostomy, ideally before 8 weeks of age
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is always pathological; outcomes are best when the Kasai procedure is performed early.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 7-year-old has fever, vomiting, jaundice and tender hepatomegaly with ALT 1,200 U/L. Anti-HAV IgM is positive. What is the management?
o: Supportive care with hydration and monitoring for acute liver failure
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Hepatitis A spreads faeco-orally, causes no chronic infection; prevention by sanitation and vaccination.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 9-year-old in Karachi has fever for 8 days, abdominal pain, relative bradycardia and hepatosplenomegaly. Blood culture grows Salmonella Typhi resistant to ceftriaxone, ampicillin, chloramphenicol, co-trimoxazole and fluoroquinolones. What is the appropriate treatment?
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Pakistan has extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid outbreaks since 2016; typhoid conjugate vaccine is in the EPI schedule.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 6-year-old has abdominal pain and vomiting and passes a long round worm in stool. Ultrasound shows a bolus of worms causing partial intestinal obstruction. What is the management?
o: Conservative management (NG decompression, IV fluids), then albendazole/mebendazole once obstruction settles
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Anthelmintics during complete obstruction may worsen impaction; surgery for failure of conservative management or perforation.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: An 8-year-old has bloody mucoid diarrhoea; stool microscopy shows trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells. What is the treatment?
o: Metronidazole followed by a luminal amoebicide
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites with ingested RBCs are diagnostic; treat contacts/carriers with luminal agents.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: After an episode of rotavirus gastroenteritis, a 2-year-old continues to have explosive watery acidic stools with perianal excoriation whenever milk is given. Stool pH is 5 with positive reducing substances. What is the diagnosis?
git-iii/paediatrics.e: Temporary lactase deficiency after mucosal injury; usually resolves in a few weeks; continue breastfeeding.

git-iii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old has chronic diarrhoea, abdominal distension, wasted buttocks and faltering growth since weaning onto wheat. Which initial test is appropriate?
o: Stool for ova and cysts only
Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA while on a gluten-containing diet
git-iii/paediatrics.e: High-titre TTG (>10× ULN) with positive EMA may allow biopsy-free diagnosis in children (ESPGHAN).

git-iii/gynaecology.s: A 24-year-old woman at 26 weeks gestation has right-sided abdominal pain, now more towards the right upper quadrant, with fever and vomiting. What is the first imaging investigation?
git-iii/gynaecology.e: The appendix is displaced upwards in pregnancy; appendicectomy should not be delayed as perforation risks fetal loss.

git-iii/gynaecology.s: A 20-year-old woman has acute right iliac fossa pain. Which investigation must be performed in every woman of reproductive age presenting with an acute abdomen?
git-iii/gynaecology.e: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst and PID all mimic appendicitis.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A 65-year-old has suspected infection with respiratory rate 24/min, systolic BP 96 mmHg and new confusion. Which bedside tool identifies him as high risk for poor outcome?
o: qSOFA score of 3 (all three criteria present)
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction due to dysregulated host response (SOFA rise ≥2); take cultures, give antibiotics within 1 hour, fluids and lactate measurement.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A farmer is brought unconscious with pinpoint pupils, excessive salivation, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia and muscle fasciculations after spraying pesticide. What is the priority drug?
o: Atropine in escalating doses until secretions dry and chest is clear, plus pralidoxime
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Death is from bronchorrhoea and respiratory failure; remove contaminated clothes, decontaminate skin, protect staff; atropine is titrated, not fixed-dose.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A 20-year-old took 25 g of paracetamol 6 hours ago. What is the appropriate management?
o: Observation for 24 hours with no antidote
Take a 4-hour (or later) paracetamol level, plot on the treatment nomogram and start N-acetylcysteine if indicated (or immediately for staggered/late presentation)
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Beyond 8 hours, start NAC while awaiting levels; King's College criteria identify those needing transplant referral (pH <7.3, INR >6.5, creatinine >3.4 mg/dL with grade III–IV encephalopathy).

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A patient after amitriptyline overdose has a QRS of 140 ms, hypotension and seizures. What is the specific treatment?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Sodium bicarbonate treats sodium channel blockade (wide QRS, arrhythmias); avoid class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics and flumazenil.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Why is flumazenil rarely used in mixed-drug overdose with benzodiazepines?
o: It can precipitate seizures, especially with co-ingested tricyclics or in chronic benzodiazepine users
It has no effect on benzodiazepine receptors
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Supportive airway management is usually sufficient.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A man who drank illicit alcohol has visual blurring ("snowstorm" vision), high anion gap metabolic acidosis and raised osmolar gap. What is the treatment?
o: Fomepizole (or ethanol) plus haemodialysis and folinic acid
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Methanol is metabolised to formic acid causing optic neuropathy; ethylene glycol causes oxalate crystals and renal failure (treated similarly with thiamine/pyridoxine).

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A family is brought from a room with a gas heater with headache, nausea and confusion. SpO₂ reads 98% on air. What is the treatment?
o: High-flow 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask (hyperbaric oxygen in selected severe cases)
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin; measure COHb on a co-oximeter; consider delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A farmer bitten by a viper 2 hours ago has local swelling, gum bleeding and a non-clotting 20-minute whole blood clotting test. What is the management?
o: Antivenom only if the snake is identified
IV polyvalent antivenom with monitoring for anaphylaxis, plus tetanus prophylaxis and limb immobilisation
Tourniquet and incision of the bite site
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Antivenom is indicated for systemic envenomation (coagulopathy, neurotoxicity, shock); avoid tight tourniquets, cutting or suction. Neurotoxic (cobra/krait) bites may need neostigmine and ventilation.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A patient with a scorpion sting has severe local pain, sweating, hypertension, tachycardia and pulmonary oedema. Which drug is used for the autonomic storm in severe envenomation?
o: Prazosin (alpha-blocker) with supportive care and scorpion antivenom where available
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Prazosin reduces mortality in severe scorpion envenomation; myocarditis and pulmonary oedema are the main causes of death.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A labourer collapses in 45°C heat with core temperature 41.5°C, confusion and hot dry skin. What is the immediate priority?
o: Rapid cooling (cold water immersion or evaporative cooling) with airway, breathing and circulation support
IV paracetamol as the main treatment
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Antipyretics do not work in heat stroke; complications include rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC and hepatic failure.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: After successful treatment of anaphylaxis, which is the most important discharge measure?
o: Prescribe an adrenaline auto-injector with training, and refer to an allergy specialist
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Serum mast cell tryptase supports the diagnosis; observe for biphasic reactions; provide a written emergency plan.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: An HIV-positive patient has CD4 count 90 cells/mm³. Which prophylaxis is indicated?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Cotrimoxazole for CD4 <200; azithromycin for MAC when CD4 <50 in some settings; ART is the key intervention.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A doctor sustains a deep needle-stick injury from a patient with untreated HIV. What is the correct action?
o: Squeeze the wound and apply bleach
No action if the doctor is vaccinated against hepatitis B
Wash the wound, report immediately and start antiretroviral PEP ideally within 2 hours (and no later than 72 hours) for 28 days
Start PEP after the source result in 1 week
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Also assess hepatitis B (vaccine/HBIG) and hepatitis C (follow-up PCR); baseline and follow-up testing are essential.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: An HIV-positive patient with CD4 60 is diagnosed with pulmonary TB. When should antiretroviral therapy be started?
o: Within 2 weeks of starting anti-TB treatment
Simultaneously on day 1 in all patients
Only if CD4 falls below 50 after ATT
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Early ART reduces mortality when CD4 <50; watch for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome; rifampicin interacts with many ART drugs (dolutegravir dose adjustment).

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: An abattoir worker in Pakistan has fever, myalgia, thrombocytopenia, deranged LFTs and bleeding gums 4 days after slaughtering animals for Eid. What infection control measure is essential?
o: Strict barrier nursing/contact isolation as CCHF is transmissible by blood and body fluids
Isolation only after confirmation by culture
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: CCHF is a tick-borne nairovirus endemic in Pakistan; ribavirin is used in some protocols; nosocomial transmission is a major hazard.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which feature in a patient with dengue indicates the need for hospital admission?
o: Rash on day 5 with stable vitals and good oral intake
Persistent vomiting with abdominal pain and a rising haematocrit as the fever settles
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Critical phase begins around defervescence (day 3–7); warning signs include mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly and rising Hct with falling platelets.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: After wading through flood water, a man develops fever, severe myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice and AKI. What is the treatment?
o: IV penicillin or ceftriaxone (doxycycline for mild disease)
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Weil disease is severe leptospirosis; a Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction may follow the first antibiotic dose.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A 23-year-old unvaccinated man has fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a descending maculopapular rash. Which complication is most common in adults?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Also otitis media, encephalitis and late SSPE; vitamin A supplementation and isolation are indicated.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A 30-year-old immunocompetent adult presents within 24 hours of a vesicular rash typical of chickenpox. What is the recommended management?
o: Oral aciclovir (adults have higher complication risk) and isolation
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Pneumonitis is the commonest serious complication in adults (especially smokers and pregnant women); VZIG for exposed high-risk contacts.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which practice best reflects antimicrobial stewardship?
o: Giving antibiotics for viral upper respiratory infection to satisfy patients
Reviewing antibiotics at 48–72 hours to de-escalate based on culture results and switch IV to oral when appropriate
Using broad-spectrum antibiotics for all fevers
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Pakistan has very high antimicrobial resistance rates; surgical prophylaxis should usually be a single preoperative dose.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which intervention most effectively reduces catheter-associated urinary tract infection?
o: Avoiding unnecessary catheterisation and removing the catheter as early as possible
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Aseptic insertion, closed drainage, keeping the bag below bladder level and daily review of need are key measures.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: An alcoholic patient develops confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. What must be given before any glucose infusion?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Glucose without thiamine precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy; untreated it progresses to Korsakoff psychosis.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A malnourished patient has a photosensitive pigmented dermatitis on sun-exposed areas ("Casal's necklace"), diarrhoea and dementia. Which deficiency is responsible?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Pellagra: the 3 Ds; occurs with maize-based diets, isoniazid therapy, alcoholism and carcinoid syndrome.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A child in a refugee camp has night blindness with Bitot's spots. What is the recommended treatment?
o: High-dose vitamin A on days 1, 2 and 14
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Xerophthalmia progresses to corneal ulceration and keratomalacia (blindness); vitamin A also reduces measles mortality.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which is the most effective public health measure to prevent iodine deficiency disorders in Pakistan?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Iodine deficiency causes goitre, hypothyroidism and cretinism; salt iodisation is the WHO-recommended strategy.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: An 82-year-old has had 3 falls in 6 months. Which intervention has the strongest evidence to reduce further falls?
o: Multifactorial assessment with strength and balance exercise training and medication review
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Review culprit drugs (benzodiazepines, antihypertensives, anticholinergics), vision, footwear, home hazards, vitamin D status and postural hypotension.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: An 80-year-old on 11 medicines has dizziness and constipation. Which tool helps identify potentially inappropriate prescribing in older adults?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Deprescribing reduces adverse drug events; anticholinergic burden contributes to falls and cognitive impairment.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which best describes comprehensive geriatric assessment?
o: A single physician's history and examination
A multidimensional, multidisciplinary assessment of medical, functional, psychological and social needs with a coordinated care plan
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: CGA improves the likelihood of older patients being alive and in their own home after admission.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A patient with metastatic cancer on regular oral morphine 30 mg twice daily has breakthrough pain. What is the appropriate rescue dose?
o: 10 mg immediate-release morphine (about one-sixth of the total daily dose) as needed
Increase the regular dose to 120 mg immediately
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Total daily dose 60 mg; breakthrough dose = 1/10–1/6 of daily dose; always co-prescribe a laxative and antiemetic as needed.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A patient with end-stage lung cancer has distressing breathlessness despite oxygen. Which drug is most appropriate?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Opioids reduce the sensation of breathlessness; benzodiazepines help associated anxiety; use a fan and positioning.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A family asks you not to tell their father that he has terminal cancer. What is the best approach?
o: Explore the family's concerns, and sensitively determine how much the patient himself wishes to know
Tell the patient everything immediately regardless of his wishes
Agree to withhold all information permanently
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Patient autonomy is central, but information should be paced to the patient's wishes; collusion harms trust and planning.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which statement about decisions not to attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation is correct?
o: Families can demand CPR that is futile
DNAR means withdrawal of all other treatment
Junior doctors should decide alone without discussion
CPR should not be offered when it would not work; the decision must be discussed with the patient (or family if the patient lacks capacity) and documented
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR; all other appropriate care continues.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which is a prerequisite before performing brainstem death testing?
o: A flat EEG is mandatory in all countries
Presence of spinal reflexes excludes brain death
Exclusion of reversible causes: hypothermia, sedatives/neuromuscular blockers, severe electrolyte or endocrine disturbance
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Tests include pupillary, corneal, oculovestibular, gag/cough reflexes and apnoea test, performed by two suitably qualified doctors.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A patient with multiple myeloma has nephrotic syndrome, macroglossia, periorbital purpura and heart failure with thickened ventricles. What is the diagnosis and diagnostic test?
o: AL amyloidosis; tissue biopsy showing apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarised light
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Abdominal fat pad or bone marrow biopsy is often used; treatment targets the underlying plasma cell clone.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A 50-year-old man has fatigue, bronze skin, diabetes, arthropathy of the 2nd/3rd MCP joints and raised ferritin with transferrin saturation of 70%. What is the treatment?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Hereditary haemochromatosis (HFE C282Y); screen for cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; chelation is used if venesection is not tolerated.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which of the following is a notifiable/reportable occupational disease relevant to industrial workers?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Occupational history ("What is your job? Any exposure to dust, chemicals, animals?") is essential in respiratory and skin disease.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which structured approach is recommended for brief tobacco cessation advice in clinics?
o: The 5 A's: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Even brief advice increases quit rates; combine behavioural support with pharmacotherapy.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which vaccine is specifically recommended for an adult with asplenia?
o: Pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY and B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Asplenic patients also need annual influenza vaccine and antibiotic prophylaxis.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A patient has been on prednisolone 20 mg daily for 4 months and wants to stop. What is the correct advice?
o: Taper gradually because of hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis suppression
Stop on alternate days without tapering
Switch to an equivalent dose of dexamethasone indefinitely
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Abrupt withdrawal after >3 weeks of significant doses risks adrenal crisis; also monitor for osteoporosis, diabetes, infections and cataract.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which drug combination most increases the risk of dangerous hyperkalaemia in a patient with CKD?
o: ACE inhibitor with spironolactone and trimethoprim
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Trimethoprim blocks the epithelial sodium channel (amiloride-like effect); monitor potassium after starting.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A patient is given a tenfold overdose of insulin due to a prescription error and becomes hypoglycaemic but recovers. What is the correct professional action?
o: Alter the notes to avoid litigation
Blame the nurse who administered it
Treat the patient, be open and honest with the patient/family about what happened, apologise, and report through the incident system
Report only if the family asks
Do not mention it because the patient recovered
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Duty of candour: explain, apologise, and use system-level analysis to prevent recurrence.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which antibiotic requires dose adjustment in significant renal impairment?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Renally cleared drugs (aminoglycosides, vancomycin, most beta-lactams except ceftriaxone, fluconazole) need adjustment with therapeutic monitoring where available.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: A severely malnourished patient started on full feeding develops confusion, arrhythmia and weakness on day 3. Which electrolyte abnormality is characteristic?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Start feeding at low energy, give thiamine before feeding and monitor/replace electrolytes daily.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which intervention best improves long-term control in a patient with multiple chronic diseases?
o: Adding more medicines at each visit
Structured patient education with a shared care plan and regular follow-up
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Self-management support and adherence review outperform escalating pharmacotherapy alone.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which statement about a screening test is correct?
o: A test with high sensitivity is preferred for screening because it minimises false negatives
Positive predictive value is independent of disease prevalence
High specificity alone makes a test suitable for screening
Screening should be offered for all diseases regardless of treatment availability
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Wilson–Jungner criteria: important condition, recognisable latent stage, acceptable test, available treatment, cost-effectiveness.

multisystem-ii/medicine.s: Which disease must be notified to public health authorities immediately in Pakistan under IHR/IDSR?
multisystem-ii/medicine.e: Other notifiable conditions include cholera, measles, dengue, CCHF, neonatal tetanus and COVID-19 under national surveillance.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 6-week-old has a temperature of 38.5°C with no focus on examination. What is the appropriate management?
o: Full septic screen (blood, urine, CSF) and empirical IV antibiotics with admission
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Infants <3 months (especially <1 month) with fever are high risk for serious bacterial infection; NICE traffic light system guides older infants.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old has fever, a rapidly spreading non-blanching purpuric rash, cold peripheries and drowsiness. What is the immediate action?
o: Give IV/IM ceftriaxone immediately and fluid resuscitate while arranging urgent transfer
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Do not delay antibiotics for investigations; notify public health; ciprofloxacin/rifampicin prophylaxis for close contacts.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 2-year-old swallowed kerosene 1 hour ago and is coughing with tachypnoea. What is contraindicated?
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Hydrocarbons cause chemical pneumonitis on aspiration; management is supportive; steroids and prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old swallowed a coin-shaped object 2 hours ago. X-ray shows a "double ring/halo" sign in the oesophagus. What is the management?
o: Observe for 24 hours for spontaneous passage
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Oesophageal button batteries cause caustic injury and perforation within hours; honey may be given as a temporising measure in children >12 months.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 3-year-old ingested her mother's iron tablets and now has vomiting, haematemesis, abdominal pain and metabolic acidosis. What is the antidote?
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Charcoal does not bind iron; whole bowel irrigation may help; a latent phase can be followed by shock and hepatic failure.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 4-year-old has scalds over the whole of one arm and the front of the trunk. Using the Lund–Browder chart, why is the rule of nines modified in children?
o: Surface area does not matter in children
Children have a proportionally larger head and smaller legs than adults
Burns are always superficial in children
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Assess for non-accidental injury with scalds in typical patterns (glove/stocking, immersion lines) and delayed presentation.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 5-year-old rescued from a canal is unresponsive and not breathing. What is the first step in resuscitation?
o: Give 5 rescue breaths before starting chest compressions
Warm the child before any resuscitation
Perform abdominal thrusts to expel water
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Drowning causes hypoxic arrest — ventilation first; continue resuscitation in hypothermia ("not dead until warm and dead").

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: Which measure most effectively reduces childhood injury deaths from road traffic crashes?
o: Waiting until children are older to teach road safety
Providing first aid kits at home
Correct use of child restraints/helmets and speed control legislation
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Injury is a leading cause of death in children over 1 year; prevention combines legislation, environment and education.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: Which statement about exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months is correct?
o: It increases the risk of obesity later
It reduces diarrhoea and respiratory infection risk and provides all required nutrients including water
Extra water is needed in hot climates
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: WHO: exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, then complementary feeding with continued breastfeeding to 2 years or beyond.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: At what age should complementary feeding normally begin, and with what consistency?
o: At 4 months with cow's milk as the main food
At 6 months, starting with thick, soft, energy-dense foods 2–3 times per day
At 9 months with family food only
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Responsive feeding, hygiene, iron-rich foods and continued breastfeeding are essential to prevent stunting.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A child's weight-for-age has crossed downwards from the 50th to below the 3rd centile over 6 months. What does this indicate?
o: Faltering growth requiring assessment of feeding, illness and psychosocial factors
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Serial measurements are more informative than a single point; assess diet, chronic disease (TB, coeliac, CF), neglect and micronutrient deficiency.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: At what temperature range should most routine EPI vaccines be stored at the health facility?
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Freezing damages adsorbed vaccines (pentavalent, hepatitis B, tetanus toxoid); use vaccine vial monitors and shake test.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 9-month-old has received only BCG and OPV-0. What is the correct approach?
o: Restart the entire schedule from the beginning
Resume the schedule from where it stopped without restarting the whole course, giving due vaccines at the same visit
Give all doses in one day at monthly intervals only
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: "A missed dose is not a missed opportunity to restart" — catch-up schedules maintain intervals; multiple injections in one visit are safe.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 9-year-old has fever and painful bilateral parotid swelling obscuring the angle of the jaw. Which complication should be discussed with the parents?
o: Aseptic meningitis and orchitis (in post-pubertal males)
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Mumps is preventable with MMR; management is supportive; avoid sour foods.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 5-year-old with chickenpox develops fever again on day 5 with a painful, rapidly spreading red swelling on the thigh. What complication is likely?
o: Secondary bacterial infection (group A streptococcal cellulitis/necrotising fasciitis)
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome) and NSAIDs (may increase risk of severe soft tissue infection); aciclovir for high-risk children.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 4-year-old from an endemic area has fever, impaired consciousness and Plasmodium falciparum on the blood film. What is the treatment of choice?
o: IV artesunate followed by a full course of oral artemisinin-based combination therapy
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Also check and treat hypoglycaemia, anaemia and convulsions; artesunate reduces mortality compared with quinine (AQUAMAT).

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: A 5-year-old stung by a scorpion has severe local pain, profuse sweating, vomiting, tachycardia and priapism. What is the key management?
o: Supportive care with analgesia, prazosin for autonomic storm and monitoring for myocarditis/pulmonary oedema (antivenom where indicated)
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Children are at higher risk of severe systemic envenomation; monitor in hospital.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: Which advice most reduces the risk of sudden infant death syndrome?
o: Place the baby supine ("back to sleep") in a smoke-free environment, avoiding bed-sharing after alcohol/sedatives, with feet to foot of cot
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Breastfeeding and room-sharing (without bed-sharing) reduce risk.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: Which principle should guide care of a child with cerebral palsy and learning disability?
o: Focus only on curing the impairment
Multidisciplinary, family-centred care focused on function, participation and inclusion
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Includes physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, nutrition, seizure control, orthopaedic care and carer support.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: What is the correct dose of intramuscular adrenaline for a 5-year-old (18 kg) with anaphylaxis?
o: 150 micrograms (0.15 mL of 1:1000) IM into the anterolateral thigh
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Doses: <6 years 150 mcg; 6–12 years 300 mcg; >12 years and adults 500 mcg; repeat every 5 minutes as needed.

multisystem-ii/paediatrics.s: Which is the most effective measure to prevent childhood poisoning at home?
o: Keeping medicines in a handbag on the floor
Keeping kerosene in soft drink bottles for easy identification
Storing medicines and chemicals in original, labelled, child-resistant containers out of reach
multisystem-ii/paediatrics.e: Storing kerosene/chemicals in beverage bottles is a common cause of paediatric poisoning in Pakistan.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: Which is one of the three phases of the WHO surgical safety checklist?
o: "Ward round" on the morning of surgery
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: Sign in (before anaesthesia), Time out (before incision), Sign out (before leaving theatre); the checklist reduces morbidity and mortality.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: A trauma patient has hypothermia 34°C, pH 7.1 and coagulopathy after major abdominal injury. What is the appropriate surgical strategy?
o: Damage control surgery: control haemorrhage and contamination, pack and temporarily close, resuscitate in ICU, return for definitive repair
Perform elective colostomy reversal at the same time
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: The "lethal triad" of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy demands abbreviated surgery with physiological restoration first.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: In major haemorrhage, which transfusion strategy is recommended?
o: Balanced ratio of red cells, plasma and platelets (approximately 1:1:1) with tranexamic acid given early
Crystalloid only until Hb falls below 5 g/dL
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: Also prevent hypothermia, correct calcium (citrate toxicity) and use point-of-care coagulation testing where available.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: After massive resuscitation for pancreatitis, a patient has a tense distended abdomen, rising airway pressures, oliguria and intra-abdominal pressure of 28 mmHg. What is the definitive management?
o: Decompressive laparotomy after failure of medical measures
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: Medical measures: sedation, nasogastric/rectal decompression, avoiding excess fluids, neuromuscular blockade; IAP >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction defines ACS.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: A patient has a deep dog bite on the forearm 3 hours ago. What is the correct wound care?
o: Primary suturing of all bite wounds
Copious irrigation and debridement, leaving the wound open (delayed closure), plus antibiotic prophylaxis (co-amoxiclav), tetanus and rabies prophylaxis
Close the wound and give steroids
Apply chili/turmeric to the wound as commonly practised
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: Bite wounds are contaminated (Pasteurella, anaerobes); facial wounds may be closed primarily after thorough cleaning.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: In which container should used needles and scalpel blades be discarded?
o: Any bin in the treatment room
Puncture-resistant sharps container, without recapping needles
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: Colour coding varies locally, but sharps always require rigid puncture-proof containers; needle-stick injuries are commonly caused by recapping.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: What is the recommended preoperative fasting time for clear fluids in an adult undergoing elective surgery?
o: 2 hours for clear fluids (6 hours for solids)
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: Prolonged fasting causes dehydration and discomfort; enhanced recovery protocols include carbohydrate loading.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: Which is a component of enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocols?
o: Routine nasogastric tubes and prolonged bed rest
Early mobilisation and early oral feeding with multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia
Routine bowel preparation for all colorectal cases
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: ERAS reduces complications and hospital stay.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: Which measure most reduces surgical site infection?
o: Shaving the site with a razor the night before
Appropriate timing of a single preoperative antibiotic dose (within 60 minutes of incision) with normothermia and glycaemic control
Avoiding hair removal entirely even when it obstructs surgery
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: Razor shaving increases SSI (use clippers immediately before surgery); maintain normothermia and glucose control.

multisystem-ii/surgery.s: Which statement about deceased organ donation is correct?
o: Donation is prohibited by all religions
Organs can be retrieved without any consent
It requires confirmation of death (brainstem or circulatory criteria) and consent according to national law and family discussion
Only living donation is legal anywhere
multisystem-ii/surgery.e: Pakistan's Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act regulates donation and prohibits commercial dealing in organs.

multisystem-ii/psychiatry.s: Which screening tool is recommended to identify hazardous and harmful drinking in a clinic setting?
multisystem-ii/psychiatry.e: CAGE is a brief alternative; brief interventions reduce consumption in hazardous drinkers.

multisystem-ii/psychiatry.s: A 28-year-old with heroin dependence wants treatment. What is the evidence-based management?
o: Opioid substitution therapy (methadone or buprenorphine) with psychosocial support
Naltrexone without any psychosocial support as first choice
multisystem-ii/psychiatry.e: OST reduces mortality, injecting risk behaviour and blood-borne virus transmission; offer hepatitis B vaccination and HIV/HCV testing.

multisystem-ii/gynaecology.s: A woman attends repeatedly with vague symptoms and unexplained bruises; her husband answers all questions for her. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ignore as a private family matter
Interview her alone in a private setting, ask directly and sensitively about safety, document findings and offer support/referral
Ask the husband for an explanation
Insist she reports to the police immediately
multisystem-ii/gynaecology.e: WHO recommends enquiry when clinical indicators are present, with first-line "LIVES" support: Listen, Inquire, Validate, Enhance safety, Support.

multisystem-ii/gynaecology.s: A 30-year-old woman with severe rheumatic mitral stenosis and pulmonary hypertension needs highly effective contraception. Which method is most appropriate?
o: Copper IUD with heavy periods in an anticoagulated patient
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system or progestogen implant
multisystem-ii/gynaecology.e: Pregnancy carries high maternal risk in pulmonary hypertension; combined hormonal methods are contraindicated (VTE risk).
